encyclopedia.title: NCCL Timeout Cascade from Single Rank Failure
encyclopedia.text: NCCL Timeout Cascade from Single Rank Failure Distributed Communication NCCL timeout detected on >50% of ranks in the job One rank consistently has the earliest error timestamp All downstream errors are identical NCCL timeout messages No independent errors on the downstream ranks. They only timed out waiting nccl cascade timeout distributed collective barrier root-cause Single GPU/rank fails (OOM, Xid, host crash) All other ranks wait at the next collective barrier for the failed rank NCCL watchdog timeout fires on every waiting rank simultaneously Logs show NCCL timeout detected on X/Y ranks where Y is most of the cluster A single root cause rank encountered a genuine failure (GPU OOM, Xid 31/79, host OOM killer, network link down) All other ranks are healthy. They only timed out because they were waiting for the failed rank at the collective barrier The cascade is not a network issue. It is a mathematical certainty: all ranks must participate in every collective

encyclopedia.title: CUDA Memory Fragmentation OOM
encyclopedia.text: CUDA Memory Fragmentation OOM GPU Memory Management CUDA OOM error showing Reserved: X, Allocated: Y, Free: Z where Free > requested size Error occurs on the same iteration every run (deterministic fragmentation pattern) expandable_segments or memory fragmentation mentioned in error context OOM happens during forward pass on large tensors, not during initialization cuda oom fragmentation memory pytorch allocator expandable-segments PyTorch reports CUDA out of memory despite total free memory being sufficient Error shows Reserved >> Allocated with Free memory still available Training fails on large tensor allocations (e.g., attention scores, activation checkpoints) Reducing batch size does not always help because the issue is fragmentation, not capacity PyTorch caching allocator reserves memory in fixed-size segments; freed segments of different sizes create a fragmented heap A large contiguous allocation (e.g., attention score matrix) cannot fit in any single free segment Without expandable segments, the allocator cannot grow an existing segment to satisfy the request Variable sequence length training creates differently-sized activation tensors each iteration, accelerating fragmentation

encyclopedia.text: GPU Uncorrectable ECC Memory Error (Xid 48/94/95) GPU Memory dmesg shows Xid 48, 94, or 95 with ECC error context nvidia-smi -q -d ECC shows non-zero Aggregate Uncorrectable errors GPU memory bandwidth may degrade as bad rows are remapped NCCL timeouts or CUDA errors may follow as downstream effects gpu ecc memory hbm xid hardware rma row-remap correctable uncorrectable GPU memory controller detected a double-bit error that ECC cannot correct Xid 48, 94, or 95 logged to dmesg GPU may trigger row remap to map out defective memory cells Persistent uncorrectable ECC errors indicate physical HBM wear-out HBM3 memory cells wear out under sustained high temperature and voltage stress, transitioning from correctable (single-bit) to uncorrectable (double-bit) ECC errors Manufacturing defects in HBM stack may cause early-life uncorrectable ECC failures Temperature-induced voltage/frequency scaling amplifies timing margin violations in HBM I/O

encyclopedia.text: NVIDIA Xid 48. ECC Uncorrectable Memory Error Hardware dmesg: Xid 48 (hardware damage) on GPU X nvidia-smi -q -d ECC shows non-zero uncorrectable error count Loss degrades silently without an explicit crash as Xid 48 corrupts weights during training ECC error count increases over time on specific GPUs xid ecc gpu hardware nvidia memory Training job terminates with Xid 48 in dmesg or nvidia-smi The same training config works on some GPUs but not others Silent data corruption: training continues but produces garbage output Single-bit ECC errors accumulate silently until a double-bit ECC error triggers Xid 48 CUDA kernels read corrupted data and propagate errors through the computation Xid 48 can corrupt model weights mid-training, producing silent data corruption The failing GPU must be identified and drained immediately

encyclopedia.title: CUDA Device Assertion Failure
encyclopedia.text: CUDA Device Assertion Failure Hardware RuntimeError: CUDA error: device-side assert triggered at /pytorch/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/.. The same training config crashes on some GPUs but not others in the same cluster nvidia-smi shows Xid errors (14, 48, 64) associated with the failing GPU CUDA kernel launches succeed but produce garbage output before triggering the assertion device-assert cuda hardware gpu ecc xid nvlink Training crashes with 'CUDA error: device-side assert triggered' and no further context The error is non-reproducible: restarting on different GPUs may succeed The assertion provides no information about which kernel or tensor triggered it Single-bit or double-bit ECC error in GPU memory corrupts tensor data during a kernel operation, causing an assertion in downstream operations (e.g., index out of bounds in embedding lookup) NVLink transaction failure corrupts data transferred between GPUs in the same node, detected by a device-side bounds check GPU memory channel degradation causes intermittent bit flips that only manifest under specific memory access patterns GPU clock or voltage instability from aging hardware causes computation errors in CUDA cores during sustained high utilization

encyclopedia.title: NCCL Watchdog Timeout due to Uneven Dataset Sharding
encyclopedia.text: NCCL Watchdog Timeout due to Uneven Dataset Sharding Data Training hangs indefinitely after a specific number of epochs or steps. One rank finishes early and exits, while others are stuck at an all_reduce barrier. Rank Desync / Straggler RuntimeError: Watchdog caught collective operation timeout NCCL WARN local rank * failed to connect to ring When sharding datasets across multiple workers, if the total number of samples is not perfectly divisible by the world size and drop_last=False, some ranks will have fewer batches. These ranks will finish their loop early, while the remaining ranks enter a collective operation (e.g., gradient all_reduce) expecting participation from all ranks, leading to a hang until the watchdog times out.

These ranks will finish their loop early, while the remaining ranks enter a collective operation (e.g., gradient all_reduce) expecting participation from all ranks, leading to a hang until the watchdog times out.

encyclopedia.title: Watchdog Timeout Caused by Silent Single-Rank OOM
encyclopedia.text: Watchdog Timeout Caused by Silent Single-Rank OOM Memory Training stops progressing, GPU utilization on some nodes drops to 0%, while others stay at 100% waiting. Watchdog timeout is reported on surviving nodes, but the actual OOM error is buried in the logs of a single rank. Crash leading to Watchdog Timeout Watchdog caught collective operation timeout CUDA out of memory RuntimeError: NCCL error in: ... unhandled system error A single rank hits a CUDA Out of Memory error during the forward or backward pass and crashes or raises an exception. Because the process group isn't cleanly torn down, the surviving ranks continue to the next all_reduce or all_gather and wait indefinitely for the dead rank. The watchdog timeout is the only visible failure on the surviving ranks.

encyclopedia.title: NCCL Watchdog Timeout due to Incorrect Network Interface
encyclopedia.text: NCCL Watchdog Timeout due to Incorrect Network Interface Network Training hangs immediately upon starting, during init_process_group or the very first collective operation. The hang lasts exactly as long as the timeout configured in init_process_group. NCCL Network Initialization Hang Watchdog caught collective operation timeout NCCL WARN Call to connect returned Connection refused Nodes have multiple network interfaces (e.g., a high-speed InfiniBand/RoCE interface, a standard ethernet interface, and a Docker bridge). NCCL heuristically picks an interface, often picking a local virtual interface (like docker0) that cannot route traffic to other nodes. Processes attempt to form the NCCL ring but packets are dropped, leading to a hang.

encyclopedia.text: Watchdog Timeout from Inconsistent Tensor Shapes Software Training hangs randomly in the middle of an epoch. Only happens with specific dynamic batch size configurations or sequence lengths. Collective API Desync Watchdog caught collective operation timeout NCCL WARN Cuda failure 'invalid argument' Ranks attempt to perform an all_gather or all_reduce on tensors that have different shapes across different ranks (e.g., dynamic sequence lengths in NLP). NCCL expects the byte count of the transferred buffers to match perfectly. When they don't, the internal state machine of NCCL gets deadlocked waiting for data that will never arrive.

encyclopedia.title: Misaligned TCPStore and NCCL Initialization Timeouts
encyclopedia.text: Misaligned TCPStore and NCCL Initialization Timeouts Environment Initialization fails on very large clusters before training even starts. Some ranks load checkpoints very slowly, causing faster ranks to timeout waiting for them in init_process_group. Initialization Timeout RuntimeError: Socket Timeout DistBackendError: Watchdog caught collective operation timeout During init_process_group, PyTorch uses a TCPStore to exchange initial connection information (like ncclUniqueId). The default timeout for TCPStore is often shorter than the NCCL watchdog or the time it takes for a massive model checkpoint to load from network storage. Fast ranks finish loading and wait at the barrier; slow ranks take too long, and the fast ranks trigger a timeout error.

encyclopedia.title: NCCL Vendor Err 129 (RDMA Timeout)
encyclopedia.text: NCCL Vendor Err 129 (RDMA Timeout) Network Training hangs completely during distributed collective operations (e.g., all_reduce). Eventually times out and crashes the training job. Occurs intermittently under heavy network load, rather than at startup. RoCEv2 Communication Timeout NCCL WARN Call to ibv_poll_cq() failed with error 12 NCCL WARN NET/IB : Got completion with error 12, opcode 0, len 0, vendor err 129 Watchdog caught collective operation timeout Vendor Error 129 represents an InfiniBand transport retry counter exceeded error. In a RoCEv2 environment, this typically happens because the network is lossy and packets are being dropped by the switch due to congestion. RoCEv2 requires a lossless fabric (via Priority Flow Control / PFC) or properly configured congestion control (DCQCN). When packets drop, the NIC retries sending until the retry limit is hit, yielding error 129.

Increase the InfiniBand timeout to tolerate minor congestion. export NCCL_IB_TIMEOUT=22 Increases the hardware retry timeout on the NIC, giving the network more time to clear congestion before throwing an error.

encyclopedia.title: NVLS Illegal Memory Access (CUDA Error 700)
encyclopedia.text: NVLS Illegal Memory Access (CUDA Error 700) Hardware The training script crashes abruptly with a CUDA 700 error. Occurs specifically when initiating collective communications over NVLink via the SHARP/NVLS hardware offload. The GPU state may become corrupted, requiring a system reboot to clear the CUDA context. Memory Access Violation NCCL WARN Cuda failure 700 'an illegal memory access was encountered' cudaErrorIllegalAddress NCCL WARN NVLS error NVLS (NVLink SHARP) offloads collective operations to the NVSwitch hardware. An incompatibility between the NCCL library version, the CUDA toolkit, and the NVIDIA display driver can cause incorrect memory mappings to be passed to the NVSwitch. When the switch attempts to read/write to the GPU memory space via these invalid addresses, it triggers a hard fault (Illegal Address).

encyclopedia.action: Disable NVLS hardware acceleration as a temporary workaround. export NCCL_NVLS_ENABLE=0 Forces NCCL to fall back to standard SM-based P2P communication rather than relying on the NVSwitch SHARP engine, bypassing the bug.

encyclopedia.title: PCIe ACS Blocking GPU Direct P2P
encyclopedia.text: PCIe ACS Blocking GPU Direct P2P Hardware Training does not crash, but multi-GPU scaling efficiency is severely degraded. NCCL logs show that Peer-to-Peer (P2P) transfers are disabled, and it is falling back to Shared Memory (SHM) routing through the host CPU. PCIe Configuration NCCL INFO P2P Disable NCCL INFO Using SHM instead of P2P Performance degradation during DDP training PCIe Access Control Services (ACS) is enabled in the host motherboard's BIOS or the Linux kernel. ACS forces all PCIe peer-to-peer traffic to be routed up to the Root Complex (CPU) for IOMMU translation/security checks. NCCL detects this topology and disables direct GPU-to-GPU memory transfers (P2P) because routing through the root complex destroys performance and can cause hardware hangs.

Apply a kernel parameter workaround to disable ACS on boot. Add `pcie_acs_override=downstream,multifunction` to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX and update-grub. Forces the Linux kernel to ignore ACS capabilities on downstream ports, allowing NCCL to re-enable P2P.

encyclopedia.title: NCCL RoCEv2 GID Index Mismatch
encyclopedia.text: NCCL RoCEv2 GID Index Mismatch Network Multi-node training hangs at the very beginning during initialization (`dist.init_process_group`). Total failure to establish cross-node GPU communication via RDMA. RoCEv2 Configuration NCCL WARN NET/IB : Got completion with error 4, opcode 0, len 0, vendor err 0 NCCL WARN node is unreachable RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet) NICs support multiple protocols simultaneously (IPv4, IPv6, RoCEv1, RoCEv2), mapped to different GID (Global Identifier) indices. By default, NCCL might attempt to use GID Index 0 (often RoCEv1 or IPv6). If the network switches are configured strictly for IPv4 RoCEv2, the packets generated by GID 0 are deemed unroutable and dropped silently.

encyclopedia.title: NCCL Binding to Virtual/Docker Interface
encyclopedia.text: NCCL Binding to Virtual/Docker Interface Network Multi-node training hangs indefinitely during `init_process_group`. Nodes cannot discover each other. Single-node multi-GPU works fine, but scaling to 2+ nodes fails. Interface Selection NCCL WARN Call to connect returned Connection timed out NCCL WARN Bootstrap : no socket interface found When multiple network interfaces are present (e.g., physical eth0, physical high-speed mlx5_0, virtual docker0, loopback), NCCL uses a heuristic to automatically select the network interface for communication. In containerized environments, it frequently selects a virtual interface like `docker0` or `flannel.1` which cannot route traffic across physical nodes.

encyclopedia.action: Explicitly define the network interface for NCCL sockets. export NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=eth0 Forces NCCL to bind to the routable physical interface, ignoring virtual bridges.

Exclude virtual interfaces using a regex exclusion. export NCCL_SOCKET_IFNAME=^docker0,lo Tells NCCL to use any interface EXCEPT the specified virtual/local ones, making the setup more resilient across heterogeneous nodes.

encyclopedia.title: DDP Hang Due to Unused Parameters in Forward Pass
encyclopedia.text: DDP Hang Due to Unused Parameters in Forward Pass Synchronization The training script completely freezes during the backward pass. No CPU or GPU utilization spikes; processes just sit idle waiting for communication. Autograd Graph Deadlock RuntimeError: Expected to have finished reduction in the prior iteration before starting a new one. Process hangs indefinitely during loss.backward() When find_unused_parameters=False (the default), DDP assumes every parameter in the model will receive a gradient. If a parameter is skipped in the forward pass (e.g., due to a conditional if-statement), its gradient is never computed. DDP waits indefinitely in the backward pass for the all-reduce operation on that missing gradient, deadlocking the training step.

encyclopedia.title: DDP Hang from Uneven Dataset Sizes Across Ranks
encyclopedia.text: DDP Hang from Uneven Dataset Sizes Across Ranks Synchronization Training hangs at the very end of an epoch. The job ultimately fails with a NCCL Watchdog Timeout after a long delay (default 30 minutes). NCCL Timeout RuntimeError: NCCL error in: ../torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp nccl timeout (Watchdog detected a stall) When using DistributedSampler without drop_last=True, the dataset size might not be perfectly divisible by the number of GPUs. Consequently, some ranks might have N batches, while others have N-1. The ranks that finish early exit the training loop, while the remaining ranks enter the next batch and block indefinitely on dist.all_reduce waiting for the finished ranks.

encyclopedia.title: SyncBatchNorm Deadlock During Single-Rank Evaluation
encyclopedia.text: SyncBatchNorm Deadlock During Single-Rank Evaluation Synchronization Training proceeds normally, but the script hangs indefinitely the moment it transitions to the validation or evaluation loop. The hang points explicitly to a batch normalization layer in stack traces. Collective Communication Deadlock Process hangs at torch.nn.SyncBatchNorm.forward NCCL Watchdog Timeout during model.eval() phase SyncBatchNorm performs an all-reduce across all processes to calculate global batch statistics. If the script only runs validation on rank 0 (a common pattern to save time), rank 0 will hit the SyncBatchNorm layer and block forever waiting for ranks 1-N, which are sitting idle. SyncBatchNorm communicates even in eval mode if not explicitly handled.

encyclopedia.title: dist.all_gather Timeout from Dynamic Tensor Shapes
encyclopedia.text: dist.all_gather Timeout from Dynamic Tensor Shapes Synchronization The script hangs during an explicit dist.all_gather() call. Usually happens when gathering outputs like variable-length sequences or dynamically detected bounding boxes. Shape Mismatch RuntimeError: NCCL error in: ../torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp Hang at dist.all_gather(tensor_list, local_tensor) dist.all_gather requires every participating rank to pass a tensor of the exact same dimensions. If Rank 0 detects 5 bounding boxes (shape [5, 4]) and Rank 1 detects 3 bounding boxes (shape [3, 4]), the underlying NCCL backend gets mismatched buffer sizes. Rather than throwing an immediate shape error, NCCL hangs indefinitely, waiting for matching sizes.

Usually happens when gathering outputs like variable-length sequences or dynamically detected bounding boxes. Shape Mismatch dist.all_gather requires every participating rank to pass a tensor of the exact same dimensions. If Rank 0 detects 5 bounding boxes (shape [5, 4]) and Rank 1 detects 3 bounding boxes (shape [3, 4]), the underlying NCCL backend gets mismatched buffer sizes. Rather than throwing an immediate shape error, NCCL hangs indefinitely, waiting for matching sizes.
encyclopedia.action: Pad tensors to a common maximum shape before gathering. max_len = max(gathered_lengths); padded_tensor = F.pad(local_tensor, (0, 0, 0, max_len - local_tensor.size(0))) Ensures all tensors passed to NCCL have identical shapes, satisfying the backend requirements.

Use built-in TensorPipe/RPC if dynamic sizes are highly variable. torch.distributed.rpc RPC is better suited for highly dynamic and asynchronous workloads than NCCL.

encyclopedia.title: Silent OOM Leading to Cluster-wide NCCL Timeout
encyclopedia.text: Silent OOM Leading to Cluster-wide NCCL Timeout Hardware A distributed training job spanning multiple nodes abruptly hangs. 30 minutes later, the job fails with a NCCL Timeout. Inspecting worker logs might reveal a CUDA Out of Memory on a single GPU on one of the nodes, while the master node only shows a timeout. Silent Crash Watchdog detected a stall NCCL WARN Cuda failure 'out of memory' One specific worker experiences a CUDA OOM (e.g., due to memory fragmentation or an unusually large sample) and crashes. PyTorch's default process group error handling doesn't forcefully abort the remaining active ranks across different nodes. The surviving ranks hit the next dist.all_reduce barrier and wait forever for the dead rank.

PyTorch's default process group error handling doesn't forcefully abort the remaining active ranks across different nodes. encyclopedia.title: System Memory OOM on FSDP Checkpoint Save
encyclopedia.text: System Memory OOM on FSDP Checkpoint Save Memory The training job suddenly gets OOM killed by the OS (dmesg shows python process killed) during the checkpoint saving phase. GPU memory looks fine, but CPU memory spikes massively right before the crash. The crash happens simultaneously across multiple nodes or local ranks. CPU OOM Killed MemoryError out of memory in torch.cat When using `FullStateDictConfig(offload_to_cpu=True)` without setting `rank0_only=True`, FSDP instructs every single rank to independently gather and reconstruct the full model parameters into its own CPU memory. For a large model and multiple ranks on a node (e.g., 8 GPUs), this creates 8 redundant copies of the full model in CPU RAM, instantly exhausting system memory.

encyclopedia.title: FSDP Ignores User-Defined NCCL Timeout with Device Mesh
encyclopedia.text: FSDP Ignores User-Defined NCCL Timeout with Device Mesh Network Long-running validation steps or checkpoint saves cause the training job to hang and then crash with a NCCL timeout exactly at 30 minutes, despite the user setting a higher timeout (e.g., 2 hours) in `init_process_group`. The issue primarily occurs when using `device_mesh` or `HYBRID_SHARD` strategies in FSDP. NCCL Timeout Watchdog caught collective operation timeout torch.distributed.DistBackendError: NCCL error in: ../torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp ncclTimeout: unhandled system error When FSDP uses `device_mesh` or certain sharding strategies like `HYBRID_SHARD`, it creates its own internal sub-process groups for inter-node and intra-node communication. These internally created process groups do not inherit the custom `timeout` specified by the user in `dist.init_process_group()`. Instead, they silently default to the standard PyTorch 30-minute timeout.

encyclopedia.title: CUDA OOM from Caching Allocator Fragmentation
encyclopedia.text: CUDA OOM from Caching Allocator Fragmentation Memory The model crashes with a CUDA OOM error. The error log states that PyTorch has a large amount of 'reserved' memory but very little 'allocated' memory (e.g., 'Tried to allocate 2.00 GiB. ... 38.00 GiB reserved'). Calculations of parameter + gradient + optimizer sizes show they should easily fit in VRAM. Fragmentation CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate... allocated and ... reserved in total by PyTorch FSDP performs frequent allocations and deallocations of varying sizes (flattening, padding, un-sharding, sharding). This usage pattern severely fragments the CUDA caching allocator. Memory gets trapped in blocks that cannot be merged, meaning PyTorch cannot find a contiguous block large enough for a new tensor, even though total free VRAM is sufficient.

Memory gets trapped in blocks that cannot be merged, meaning PyTorch cannot find a contiguous block large enough for a new tensor, even though total free VRAM is sufficient.

encyclopedia.title: FSDP Hang Due to Divergent Parameter Initialization
encyclopedia.text: FSDP Hang Due to Divergent Parameter Initialization Model Training hangs indefinitely on the first forward pass or backward pass. The hang only occurs when using `sync_module_states=True` or during the first un-sharding operation. No direct error is thrown until the NCCL watchdog times out. Initialization Mismatch Watchdog caught collective operation timeout: _ALLGATHER_BASE Process group timed out during forward pass FSDP requires all ranks to have identical model architectures and parameter shapes. If `param_init_fn` is used incorrectly (e.g., using random generation that affects tensor shapes or diverging control flow per rank), Rank 0 might have a different layer structure or shape than Rank 1. When FSDP tries to all-gather parameters, the metadata mismatches, causing NCCL to wait indefinitely for matching tensor sizes that never arrive.

encyclopedia.title: TorchElastic Rendezvous Timeout on Large Clusters
encyclopedia.text: TorchElastic Rendezvous Timeout on Large Clusters Network The distributed job fails to start, crashing after exactly 10 minutes (600 seconds). Some nodes log that they are waiting for other ranks, but the other ranks never connect. Rendezvous Failure torch.distributed.elastic.rendezvous.api.RendezvousTimeoutError Rendezvous timeout occurred as some nodes failed to join The default `torchrun` rendezvous timeout is 600 seconds. In large scale clusters (e.g., hundreds of nodes on AWS/GCP), container startup times, image pulling, and internal network resolution can easily exceed 10 minutes, causing early nodes to time out and crash before late nodes finish booting up. Additionally, short hostnames might fail to resolve if DNS is misconfigured, causing silent connection drops.

encyclopedia.title: Rank 0 OOM During ZeRO-3 Checkpoint Save
encyclopedia.text: Rank 0 OOM During ZeRO-3 Checkpoint Save Memory Training runs completely fine and stably, but suddenly crashes with a CUDA OOM precisely when attempting to save the first checkpoint. Only rank 0 experiences the Out of Memory error; other ranks sit idle or timeout. Checkpoint OOM RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate... [Rank 0] OOM encountered during save_checkpoint By default, DeepSpeed's ZeRO-3 config parameter `gather_16bit_weights_on_model_save` is often set to true. This instructs DeepSpeed to unshard and consolidate all model weights onto a single GPU (Rank 0) to save a standard fp16 model file. For massive models, gathering the entire model state on a single GPU immediately exceeds its VRAM capacity.

encyclopedia.title: Host RAM Exhaustion via ZeRO Offload Pinned Memory
encyclopedia.text: Host RAM Exhaustion via ZeRO Offload Pinned Memory Memory The training script is unexpectedly killed by the OS (OOM Killer) during initialization or early training. There are no CUDA Out of Memory errors; VRAM usage is well within limits. System RAM usage spikes to 100% just before the crash. CPU OOM Killed Exit code 137 kernel: Out of memory: Killed process When using ZeRO-Offload (CPU offloading for parameters/optimizer states), DeepSpeed enables `pin_memory: true` by default. Pinned memory (page-locked memory) cannot be swapped to disk. Offloading large states into pinned memory rapidly exhausts available physical RAM, triggering the Linux OOM killer.

encyclopedia.title: Optimizer State Load Failure on Cluster Resize
encyclopedia.text: Optimizer State Load Failure on Cluster Resize State Management Training pauses and checkpoint saves successfully, but when attempting to resume the run with a different number of GPUs, `load_checkpoint` crashes. The weights might load, but `load_optimizer_states=True` fails entirely. Checkpointing AssertionError: Expected ... to be equal to ... Missing optimizer state files RuntimeError: Error(s) in loading state_dict for... ZeRO optimizer states are heavily coupled to the exact partitioning topology (world size) present when the checkpoint was saved. If a model was trained on 8 GPUs, there are 8 sharded optimizer state files. Standard DeepSpeed loading expects a 1:1 mapping and cannot dynamically reshard the Adam states to, say, 16 GPUs.

encyclopedia.title: NCCL Hang on AllGather due to Asymmetric Data Loading
encyclopedia.text: NCCL Hang on AllGather due to Asymmetric Data Loading Network Training hangs indefinitely (usually at the very end of an epoch). GPU utilization drops to 0%, but VRAM remains allocated. After 30 minutes, a watchdog timeout trace is dumped, pointing to an `AllGather` operation in the ZeRO-3 forward pass. NCCL Timeout Watchdog caught collective operation timeout: WorkNCCL(SeqNum=...) RuntimeError: NCCL communicator was aborted nccl timeout ZeRO-3 requires all ranks to participate in collective communication (`AllGather`) to reconstruct parameter layers during the forward and backward passes. If `drop_last=False` is set in the PyTorch DataLoader, the final batch of an epoch may be uneven. A rank that receives a smaller batch (or finishes its data early) exits the training loop, while other ranks hit the `AllGather` barrier and wait indefinitely.

encyclopedia.title: Forward Pass OOM due to Excessive Parameter Prefetching
encyclopedia.text: Forward Pass OOM due to Excessive Parameter Prefetching Memory Model successfully initializes, but throws an OOM immediately upon starting the first forward pass. Reducing batch size does not resolve the OOM. The allocated memory trace points to internal DeepSpeed buffer allocations rather than activation tensors. VRAM Spike CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate ... bytes Failing at DeepSpeed parameter fetch / allgather DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 uses a `prefetch_bucket_size` (defaulting to a very large number like 50M) to preemptively AllGather upcoming layers into VRAM to hide communication latency. For large models or restricted memory hardware, pulling too many future layers into GPU memory at once overrides the savings of sharding, causing an OOM.

encyclopedia.title: Variable Sequence Length Shape Exchange Deadlock
encyclopedia.text: Variable Sequence Length Shape Exchange Deadlock Network Training hangs indefinitely on the first training step or during transition between steady-state and cooldown in the 1F1B pipeline schedule. GPU utilization drops to 0% while processes remain active. P2P Communication Process stuck in _communicate_shapes() Rank stalled in torch.distributed.irecv Watchdog timeout during pipeline parallel P2P communication When `--variable-seq-lengths` and `batch_p2p_comm=True` are enabled with Pipeline Parallelism (PP >= 4), the `_communicate_shapes()` function enforces a strict, fixed point-to-point operation ordering: [send_prev, recv_prev, send_next, recv_next]. During the transition phases of the pipeline schedule, this strict ordering causes circular waits (Rank A waiting on Rank B, while Rank B waits on Rank A for a different operation), leading to a distributed deadlock.

encyclopedia.title: MoE Expert Parallelism Comm Overlap Deadlock
encyclopedia.text: MoE Expert Parallelism Comm Overlap Deadlock Hardware/Network Training with Mixture of Experts (MoE) hangs sporadically when scaling to multiple nodes. Only occurs when `--overlap-moe-expert-parallel-comm` is enabled. NCCL Deadlock NCCL WARN [send] via NET/IB/0/GDRDMA failed NCCL INFO Call to ncclAllGather failed Hangs during MoE routing or expert collective communication The MoE overlap scheduler uses a shared CUDA event as a 'baton' to sequence communications across nodes. Due to timing variations, ranks can launch overlapping NCCL collectives in different orders (e.g., Rank 0 launches All2All_A then All2All_B, while Rank 1 launches All2All_B then All2All_A). NCCL mandates that all ranks participating in a collective must submit the collective calls in the exact same sequence. The mismatch causes a cross-rank NCCL deadlock.

encyclopedia.title: Tensor Parallel RNG State Context Divergence Deadlock
encyclopedia.text: Tensor Parallel RNG State Context Divergence Deadlock Software Training hangs during the backward pass when using Tensor Parallelism combined with activation checkpointing (recomputation). Sometimes accompanied by silent math divergence before the hang. RNG State Divergence RuntimeError: RNG state changed within GPU RNG context NCCL AllReduce timeout during backward pass Process stuck in torch.distributed.all_reduce In Tensor Parallelism (TP), ranks within the same TP group must execute identical control flows for collective operations. If the `CudaRNGStatesTracker` is misconfigured or activation offloading fails to perfectly restore the RNG state, dropout masks or stochastic operations will differ across TP ranks. This causes divergent control flow (e.g., dropping different tokens in sequence parallel), leading to ranks submitting different sequences of NCCL calls and deadlocking.

encyclopedia.title: MoE Pipeline Stage Asymmetry Hang
encyclopedia.text: MoE Pipeline Stage Asymmetry Hang Model Training initialization succeeds, but hangs indefinitely upon completing the first forward pass or when logging auxiliary losses. Occurs specifically when using custom pipeline layouts with MoE models. Pipeline Configuration Process stuck in reduce_aux_losses_tracker_across_ranks NCCL timeout waiting on rank in pipeline group When using a custom `--pipeline-model-parallel-layout`, users may configure a pipeline stage to have zero MoE layers (e.g., placing all MoE layers in the middle stages). However, the logging/loss aggregation function `reduce_aux_losses_tracker_across_ranks` implicitly assumes all ranks in the pipeline group possess MoE layers and invokes an AllReduce across the entire pipeline group. The stage with 0 MoE layers bypasses the MoE loss logic and never joins the AllReduce, causing the other stages to hang forever waiting for it.

Alternatively, patch the Megatron code to use a custom NCCL communicator that only includes ranks containing MoE layers.

encyclopedia.title: TP Comm Overlap Topology Conflict Deadlock
encyclopedia.text: TP Comm Overlap Topology Conflict Deadlock Network Training freezes unpredictably during the backward pass. Only occurs when `--tp-comm-overlap` is turned on. Usually manifests on specific hardware setups (e.g., PCIe-based multi-GPU nodes without full NVLink). Communication Overlap Watchdog caught collective operation timeout Process stuck in torch.distributed.all_reduce or custom TP overlap kernel The `--tp-comm-overlap` feature schedules communication kernels concurrently with compute kernels using separate CUDA streams. On systems lacking dense NVLink (where P2P must go through PCIe), the PCIe bus becomes saturated. This saturation delays the communication stream to the point where stream synchronization primitives (CUDA events) trigger out of order, or NCCL drops into a fallback protocol that deadlocks when interleaved with heavy compute kernels.

encyclopedia.title: Xid 13: Graphics Engine Exception due to Kernel Out-of-Bounds Access
encyclopedia.text: Xid 13: Graphics Engine Exception due to Kernel Out-of-Bounds Access Software Training script crashes abruptly with a CUDA illegal memory access error. dmesg shows NVRM Xid 13 Graphics Engine Exception. Subsequent PyTorch operations fail until the process is restarted. Xid Error NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:01:00): 13, Graphics Exception: Warp Illegal Address NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:01:00): 13, Graphics Exception: ESR 0x404490=0x80000000 RuntimeError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered A custom PyTorch C++ / CUDA kernel (or a bug in a framework like TensorRT/DeepSpeed) calculates an incorrect thread index or memory offset, resulting in a read or write operation past the allocated bounds of a tensor. The NVIDIA hardware traps this memory violation (Warp Illegal Address) and halts the GPU context, logging an Xid 13 error.

encyclopedia.title: Xid 31: Memory Page Fault from Process Resource Exhaustion
encyclopedia.text: Xid 31: Memory Page Fault from Process Resource Exhaustion Memory The GPU process hangs indefinitely or is abruptly killed by the OS. Syslog/dmesg displays an Xid 31 error indicating a memory page fault. Often occurs during heavy multi-tenancy, extreme memory pressure, or when rapidly allocating/freeing memory across multiple processes. Xid Error NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:04:00): 31, Ch 00000010, engmask 00000101, intr 10000000 GPU memory page fault kernel: NVRM: unhandled page fault Xid 31 occurs when the GPU attempts to access a virtual address that is not mapped in the GPU page tables. While this can be a kernel bug, it frequently happens under severe memory pressure or thrashing where memory is allocated but not properly bound, or an application uses an invalid pointer that falls outside its mapped VRAM range.

encyclopedia.title: Xid 43: Watchdog Timeout due to PSU Transient Spikes
encyclopedia.text: Xid 43: Watchdog Timeout due to PSU Transient Spikes Hardware Under high load (e.g., LLM training or heavy batch inference), a specific GPU stops responding. The node may completely freeze, or the affected GPU may fall off the bus entirely (leading to Xid 79). nvidia-smi hangs or reports the GPU as lost. Xid Error NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:81:00): 43, Ch 00000008, engmask 00000101 GPU stopped processing Reset Channel Verification Error During heavy compute operations, modern GPUs (like the A100 or H100) experience massive microsecond-level power spikes. If the Power Supply Unit (PSU) or the 12V PCIe power cables cannot handle the transient load, the GPU voltage drops. This physical brownout stalls the GPU clocks, tripping the internal driver watchdog timer, which reports an Xid 43 (stopped processing) and resets the channel.

encyclopedia.title: Xid 48: Double Bit ECC Error from VRAM Degradation
encyclopedia.text: Xid 48: Double Bit ECC Error from VRAM Degradation Hardware Training crashes randomly with NCCL timeouts or corrupted output tensors. dmesg logs flooded with Xid 48 Double Bit ECC errors. Sometimes accompanied by Xid 64 (Failed page retirement). Xid Error NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:03:00): 48, Double Bit ECC Error Uncorrectable ECC error encountered The physical VRAM (HBM or GDDR) on the GPU has degraded over time due to thermal stress or manufacturing defects. A double-bit error is mathematically uncorrectable by the GPU ECC engine, meaning data corruption has physically occurred in the memory cell. The driver kills the context to prevent silent data corruption.

encyclopedia.title: Xid 43: PCIe Link Training Failure Under Load
encyclopedia.text: Xid 43: PCIe Link Training Failure Under Load Hardware Server periodically logs PCIe Advanced Error Reporting (AER) errors. During multi-GPU communication (e.g. NCCL AllReduce), the GPU driver halts with Xid 43. Sometimes the GPU completely disappears from the PCIe bus (Xid 79). Xid Error NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:41:00): 43, Ch 00000000, engmask 00000101 pcieport 0000:00:03.0: AER: Corrected error received pcie bus error: severity=Corrected, type=Physical Layer, id=0018 Poor physical seating of the GPU in the PCIe slot, or a degraded PCIe riser cable, degrades signal integrity. When the system shifts into high-bandwidth PCIe Gen4/Gen5 states for inter-GPU communication, link training fails or bit errors overwhelm the error-correction. The resulting communication stall triggers the driver watchdog (Xid 43).

encyclopedia.title: NVIDIA Xid 61 - Internal Microcontroller Breakpoint
encyclopedia.text: NVIDIA Xid 61 - Internal Microcontroller Breakpoint Hardware PyTorch training jobs hang or crash unexpectedly System logs show internal microcontroller warnings nvidia-smi may still show the GPU, but it becomes unresponsive to new workloads Xid Error NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:xx:xx): 61, pid='<pid>', name=<process_name>, Internal Microcontroller Warning CUDA error: unspecified launch failure The GPU's internal processors (like the Power Management Unit or GSP) encountered a diagnostic event, such as a thermal anomaly, voltage droop, or firmware bug, and halted execution to prevent corruption.

Common causes include inadequate power supply under high load, a loose PCIe connection, faulty riser cables, or active state power management (ASPM) conflicts.

However, it successfully 'contained' the error to the specific application using that memory page, preventing a full system crash.

encyclopedia.title: Xid 48 Double-Bit ECC Error in HBM
encyclopedia.text: Xid 48 Double-Bit ECC Error in HBM Hardware PyTorch training job crashes immediately and unexpectedly. The GPU becomes completely inaccessible to new processes. nvidia-smi shows the GPU in an error state or processes fail to attach to it. Uncorrectable ECC Error RuntimeError: CUDA error: uncorrectable ECC error encountered NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:ca:00): 48, Uncorrectable double bit error A multi-bit memory error occurred in the High Bandwidth Memory (HBM) that the hardware ECC engine cannot correct. To prevent silent data corruption, the GPU driver marks this as a 'sticky' hardware error and halts all compute operations on the device.

encyclopedia.action: Reset the GPU to clear the sticky error state sudo nvidia-smi -i <GPU_UUID> -r Clearing the GPU resets its internal state, allowing it to be used again if the error was a transient single-event upset.

encyclopedia.title: Xid 63 Page Retirement Storm causing severe throttling
encyclopedia.text: Xid 63 Page Retirement Storm causing severe throttling Hardware System logs (dmesg) are flooded with hundreds of Xid 63 messages. PyTorch training throughput drops significantly (e.g., iterations per second falls by 50%+). Other nodes in the distributed training cluster timeout waiting for the affected node in NCCL operations. ECC Page Retirement NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:4a:00): 63, Row Remapper: New bad page NCCL WARN Timeout waiting for data The HBM is rapidly degrading, triggering single-bit ECC errors at an extremely high frequency. The GPU's self-healing mechanism dynamically retires and remaps these bad memory pages (Xid 63). Doing this hundreds of times per second stalls the memory controller and destroys memory bandwidth.

encyclopedia.title: HBM Silent Data Corruption leading to Loss Spikes
encyclopedia.text: HBM Silent Data Corruption leading to Loss Spikes Hardware After days or weeks of stable training, the loss curve suddenly spikes or diverges to NaN. Checkpoints saved after the spike contain poisoned weights. No Xid errors, CUDA errors, or kernel panics are logged in the system. Silent Data Corruption Loss sudden spike to NaN Gradient norm explosion without any hyperparameter changes A transient hardware fault occurred in an unprotected part of the GPU memory pipeline (e.g., a multi-bit flip that bypassed ECC, or a fault in the L1 cache/SRAM). This resulted in an incorrect matrix multiplication output (e.g., a massive floating-point value). Because it wasn't caught by hardware parity checks, the bad data silently poisoned the gradients.

encyclopedia.title: Xid 64 InfoROM Page Retirement Failure
encyclopedia.text: Xid 64 InfoROM Page Retirement Failure Hardware PyTorch cannot initialize the GPU or crashes on startup. The GPU disappears from nvidia-smi or reports an ERR state. System reboots temporarily resolve the issue, but it returns shortly after. InfoROM Failure NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:8a:00): 64, Page Retirement Failure CUDA error: all CUDA-capable devices are busy or unavailable The GPU detected a bad HBM memory page and attempted to record it in the InfoROM (EEPROM) for permanent retirement. However, the InfoROM is either full or physically degraded, preventing the page remap table from being updated. The driver halts initialization to prevent data corruption.

encyclopedia.action: Hardware replacement (RMA) N/A If the InfoROM cannot accept new bad page records, the GPU's self-healing is permanently broken. It must be returned.

encyclopedia.title: Thermal-Induced ECC Throttling causing NCCL timeouts
encyclopedia.text: Thermal-Induced ECC Throttling causing NCCL timeouts Environment During heavy All-Reduce operations, training stalls and NCCL timeouts occur. The issue consistently happens on the same physical node during peak workload. nvidia-smi shows the memory temperature (not just GPU core temp) hovering near or above 95°C. Thermal Stress on HBM NCCL WARN Call to system function posix_memalign failed NCCL WARN Timeout waiting for data Poor airflow or a dried-out thermal pad on the HBM stack causes the memory to overheat. High temperatures exponentially increase the rate of transient single-bit flips. The hardware ECC engine corrects these on the fly, but the correction logic adds severe latency to memory transactions. This memory starvation delays collective communication, ultimately causing a NCCL timeout.

encyclopedia.title: NVLink Fatal Error Xid 74 with Fabric Manager Crash
encyclopedia.text: NVLink Fatal Error Xid 74 with Fabric Manager Crash Hardware/Network Training hangs indefinitely during collective communications. nvidia-smi hangs or shows ERR! for GPU utilization. Fabric manager service status shows failed or inactive. NVLink/NVSwitch NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:10:00): 74, NVLink nvidia-fabricmanager: NVML API failed NCCL WARN NVLink connection timeout A physical NVLink transceiver issue or NVSwitch port degradation causes high error rates. The Fabric Manager attempts to isolate the port but fails due to aggressive NCCL polling, resulting in a kernel panic or an unrecoverable Xid 74 error that drops the NVLink fabric.

encyclopedia.title: PCIe AER Uncorrectable Error Dropping GPU
encyclopedia.text: PCIe AER Uncorrectable Error Dropping GPU Hardware Training job crashes with CUDA error: device-side assert triggered or CUDA_ERROR_UNKNOWN. nvidia-smi lists fewer GPUs than physically present, or shows ERR!/No devices found. System logs show a cascade of PCIe AER errors. PCIe/AER PCIe Bus Error: severity=Uncorrected (Fatal) type=Malformed TLP NVRM: GPU at PCI:0000:86:00: GPU-b2951f... has fallen off the bus. Marginal signal integrity on the PCIe riser cable or motherboard slot under heavy thermal load causes a Malformed Transaction Layer Packet (TLP). The PCIe root complex detects the fatal error via AER and isolates/resets the device, causing it to fall off the bus.

encyclopedia.action: Reseat GPU and check PCIe riser Hardware intervention required Physical connection issues are the primary cause of Malformed TLPs. Reseating or replacing the riser fixes signal integrity.
steps: Reseat GPU and check PCIe riser Hardware intervention required Physical connection issues are the primary cause of Malformed TLPs. Reseating or replacing the riser fixes signal integrity.
Lower PCIe Gen speed via BIOS Set PCIe to Gen3 in BIOS/UEFI Reduces signal frequency, improving stability on marginal links at the cost of bandwidth.

encyclopedia.title: Silent PCIe Link Speed Downgrade Under Load
encyclopedia.text: Silent PCIe Link Speed Downgrade Under Load Hardware Training throughput drops significantly (e.g., 50% slower iterations) without any crashes. Host-to-device data loading becomes the primary bottleneck in PyTorch Profiler. nvidia-smi shows low GPU utilization but high memory transfer times. PCIe/Link Training RxErr LinkCap: Port #0, Speed 16GT/s, Width x16 LinkSta: Speed 8GT/s, Width x8 Thermal expansion or microscopic dust in the PCIe slot causes transient connection issues during Active State Power Management (ASPM) or link retraining. The PCIe controller automatically negotiates a lower speed (Gen3) or narrower width (x8) to maintain stability.

encyclopedia.action: Force PCIe link retrain echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:xx:00.0/reset Forces the OS to reset the PCIe device, initiating a new link training sequence which often recovers full x16 speed.

encyclopedia.title: IOMMU DMAR Fault Causing GPU Hangs
encyclopedia.text: IOMMU DMAR Fault Causing GPU Hangs Hardware/Environment GPU stops responding to the host entirely during intensive peer-to-peer (P2P) operations. Processes accessing the GPU enter D (uninterruptible sleep) state. System may hard freeze or require a physical reboot. PCIe/IOMMU DMAR: DRHD: handling fault status reg DMAR: [DMA Read] Request device [xx:00.0] fault addr NVRM: GPU at PCI:0000:xx:00.0: RmInitAdapter failed! When GPUs attempt P2P transfers over the PCIe bus through the host's IOMMU, incorrect page table mapping or hardware bug in the CPU PCIe root complex causes a DMA access violation. The IOMMU blocks the transaction (DMAR fault), hanging the GPU's memory controller.

encyclopedia.action: Bypass IOMMU for P2P via kernel parameter intel_iommu=igfx_off iommu=pt (or amd_iommu=pt) Sets the IOMMU to pass-through mode for non-virtualized devices, preventing unnecessary DMA address translation faults for direct GPU communication.

encyclopedia.title: NCCL NVLink Routing Loop Fallback Hang
encyclopedia.text: NCCL NVLink Routing Loop Fallback Hang Software/Network Distributed training job starts fine but hangs after a specific number of steps. Strace shows processes stuck in futex waits or ibv_poll_cq. Extremely high CPU usage on rank 0. NCCL/NVLink NCCL WARN Call to cuMemcpy3DAsync failed NCCL INFO NET/IB : Got completion with error 12 NCCL WARN Ring 00 : 8 -> 0 via P2P/IPC/read A single faulty NVLink lane causes NCCL to detect topology degradation. NCCL attempts to dynamically route traffic around the bad link using InfiniBand (IB) or PCIe as a fallback. Due to a bug in older NCCL versions or complex topology configs, this fallback creates an infinite routing loop or buffer deadlock in the collective communication ring.

NCCL attempts to dynamically route traffic around the bad link using InfiniBand (IB) or PCIe as a fallback. Due to a bug in older NCCL versions or complex topology configs, this fallback creates an infinite routing loop or buffer deadlock in the collective communication ring.
encyclopedia.action: Disable P2P routing to force uniform fallback export NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1 Prevents NCCL from building complex hybrid NVLink+IB rings, forcing it to use IB uniformly, which avoids the deadlock.
steps: Disable P2P routing to force uniform fallback export NCCL_P2P_DISABLE=1 Prevents NCCL from building complex hybrid NVLink+IB rings, forcing it to use IB uniformly, which avoids the deadlock.

encyclopedia.title: PyTorch CUDA Memory Fragmentation
encyclopedia.text: PyTorch CUDA Memory Fragmentation Memory CUDA OOM exception thrown even when nvidia-smi shows plenty of total free GPU memory. The error message shows that 'reserved' memory is much larger than 'allocated' memory. Fragmentation RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate .* MiB .* .* GiB reserved in total by PyTorch reserved memory is >> allocated memory The PyTorch caching allocator reserves large blocks of memory and splits them for individual tensor allocations. Over time, memory becomes fragmented into many small blocks, preventing the allocation of a new contiguous large block, even if the total free memory across all small blocks is sufficient.
encyclopedia.anchorText: PyTorch CUDA Memory Fragmentation CUDA OOM exception thrown even when nvidia-smi shows plenty of total free GPU memory. The error message shows that 'reserved' memory is much larger than 'allocated' memory. Fragmentation The PyTorch caching allocator reserves large blocks of memory and splits them for individual tensor allocations. Over time, memory becomes fragmented into many small blocks, preventing the allocation of a new contiguous large block, even if the total free memory across all small blocks is sufficient.
encyclopedia.action: Set the maximum split size for the caching allocator to reduce fragmentation. export PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:128 This prevents the allocator from splitting blocks larger than 128MB, forcing it to reuse existing smaller blocks and keeping large blocks intact for large tensor allocations.
steps: Set the maximum split size for the caching allocator to reduce fragmentation. export PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=max_split_size_mb:128 This prevents the allocator from splitting blocks larger than 128MB, forcing it to reuse existing smaller blocks and keeping large blocks intact for large tensor allocations.

Enable expandable segments (in newer PyTorch versions). export PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF=expandable_segments:True Allows the caching allocator to allocate memory in segments that can be expanded, heavily reducing fragmentation.

encyclopedia.title: Computation Graph Memory Leak via Loss Accumulation
encyclopedia.text: Computation Graph Memory Leak via Loss Accumulation Memory Training runs fine for the first few batches/epochs, but GPU memory usage slowly climbs. Eventually throws CUDA OOM in the middle of a training loop, rather than on the first iteration. Memory Leak RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Memory usage grows linearly with each training iteration until OOM. The developer accumulates the loss tensor across batches for logging (e.g., `total_loss += loss`). Because `loss` is a PyTorch tensor attached to the computation graph, accumulating it keeps the entire computation graph for every batch in memory, preventing garbage collection.
encyclopedia.anchorText: Computation Graph Memory Leak via Loss Accumulation Training runs fine for the first few batches/epochs, but GPU memory usage slowly climbs. Eventually throws CUDA OOM in the middle of a training loop, rather than on the first iteration. Memory Leak The developer accumulates the loss tensor across batches for logging (e.g., `total_loss += loss`). Because `loss` is a PyTorch tensor attached to the computation graph, accumulating it keeps the entire computation graph for every batch in memory, preventing garbage collection.
encyclopedia.action: Detach the tensor from the computation graph before accumulating. total_loss += loss.item() Calling `.item()` converts the 0-d tensor to a standard Python float, dropping the reference to the autograd graph.

encyclopedia.title: Evaluation Loop OOM due to Missing torch.no_grad
encyclopedia.text: Evaluation Loop OOM due to Missing torch.no_grad Memory Training completes an epoch successfully, but the script crashes with CUDA OOM as soon as it enters the evaluation or testing loop. Evaluation batch size is often set larger than training batch size, exacerbating the problem. Memory Leak RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. (Occurs during the validation/evaluation phase) The evaluation loop is executing without `with torch.no_grad():` or `@torch.inference_mode()`. Therefore, PyTorch continues to build the autograd computation graph during evaluation, storing activations. Because `.backward()` is never called, the graph is never freed, leading to a massive memory spike.

encyclopedia.title: Optimizer State Memory Explosion
encyclopedia.text: Optimizer State Memory Explosion Memory The model loads fine. The forward pass runs fine. The backward pass (`loss.backward()`) completes. The process crashes immediately when `optimizer.step()` is called. Optimizer State RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. (Occurs on the line `optimizer.step()`) OOM exactly after the first backward pass is completed. Optimizers like Adam and AdamW maintain moment states (running averages of gradients and squared gradients) for every parameter. For a model with N parameters, the optimizer state requires 2 * N memory (often in FP32). The initialization of these state tensors happens lazily on the first `optimizer.step()`, suddenly doubling or tripling the memory footprint of the model weights.

encyclopedia.title: Activation Memory Explosion from Quadratic Attention
encyclopedia.text: Activation Memory Explosion from Quadratic Attention Memory Model trains fine on short texts, but crashes with CUDA OOM as soon as a batch contains long sequences. Reducing the batch size to 1 still results in an OOM error for long documents. Activation Memory RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate (large amount) MiB OOM occurs during `model(inputs)` inside a SelfAttention layer. Standard multi-head dot-product attention computes an attention matrix of size (batch_size, num_heads, seq_length, seq_length). The memory complexity is O(N^2) with respect to the sequence length. As sequence length increases, the intermediate activations saved for the backward pass become excessively large and exhaust VRAM.

encyclopedia.title: nn.Embedding Out of Bounds Illegal Memory Access
encyclopedia.text: nn.Embedding Out of Bounds Illegal Memory Access Memory The training script crashes suddenly without warning, often pointing to an arbitrary line of code (like a loss function or forward pass of a different layer). When running in a multi-GPU setup, it might trigger an NCCL timeout because one GPU goes down. The exact stack trace points to operations downstream of the embedding layer due to asynchronous CUDA execution. Out of Bounds Access RuntimeError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered block: [0,0,0], thread: [32,0,0] Assertion `index >= -sizes[i] && index < sizes[i]` failed An index passed to a PyTorch `nn.Embedding` layer exceeds the configured `num_embeddings` (e.g., passing token ID 1000 to an embedding matrix of size 1000, where max valid is 999). Because CUDA executes asynchronously, the out-of-bounds kernel memory violation doesn't throw a Python exception immediately. Instead, the GPU's memory protection fault corrupts the CUDA context, causing a subsequent operation to raise the generic 'illegal memory access' error.

encyclopedia.title: torch.multinomial Invalid Probability Memory Access
encyclopedia.text: torch.multinomial Invalid Probability Memory Access Memory Sampling steps in generative models (e.g., top-p, top-k sampling) crash randomly with illegal memory access. The crash happens deeper into training, not immediately, often right after loss spikes. Kernel Panic RuntimeError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered RuntimeError: probability tensor contains either `inf`, `nan` or element < 0 When `torch.multinomial` receives a probability distribution tensor containing `NaN` values, negative values, or all zeros, the CUDA kernel fails to build a valid Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF). This causes the sampling kernel to read/write out of bounds when attempting to perform binary search on the corrupted CDF array.

encyclopedia.title: NCCL Timeout Triggered by Hidden Illegal Memory Access
encyclopedia.text: NCCL Timeout Triggered by Hidden Illegal Memory Access Network Distributed training hangs indefinitely during an `all_reduce` or `backward` pass. One or more nodes eventually report an NCCL timeout error. No direct CUDA memory errors are immediately visible in the logs of the master node. NCCL Timeout RuntimeError: NCCL error in: /pytorch/torch/lib/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp ncclUnhandledCudaError: Call to CUDA function failed. Watchdog caught collective operation timeout: WorkNCCL A completely different, localized error (like an out-of-bounds tensor access, device-side assert, or OOM) occurred on a *single* GPU in the distributed cluster. Because that GPU's CUDA context crashes, it silently stops participating in NCCL collective communications. The other healthy GPUs block indefinitely waiting for it, eventually triggering an NCCL timeout.

encyclopedia.title: Missing GradScaler Update in AMP Loop
encyclopedia.text: Missing GradScaler Update in AMP Loop Precision Model trains normally for a few steps and then loss suddenly jumps to NaN. Weights become filled with NaN. Mixed Precision (AMP) Loss goes to NaN RuntimeError: Function 'LogSoftmaxBackward' returned nan values in its 0th output When using `torch.cuda.amp.autocast()`, gradients are computed in float16. The dynamic range of float16 is narrow, causing gradients to overflow to infinity. If a `GradScaler` is not used, or if `scaler.update()` is omitted, the scale factor isn't adjusted to prevent these overflows, leading to NaN gradients and subsequently NaN loss.

Model crashes during the optimizer step rather than the forward/backward pass. encyclopedia.title: Autograd Singularity at sqrt(0)
encyclopedia.text: Autograd Singularity at sqrt(0) Mathematics Forward pass outputs valid numbers, but loss or gradients become NaN on the backward pass. Issue occurs randomly, often when calculating pairwise distances or L2 norms that happen to perfectly align (distance = 0). Function Singularity RuntimeError: Function 'SqrtBackward' returned nan values The analytical derivative of sqrt(x) is 1 / (2 * sqrt(x)). If the input x evaluates to exactly 0, the denominator becomes 0, and the gradient evaluates to infinity. PyTorch's autograd engine will then propagate NaN back to the network's weights.

encyclopedia.text: CrossEntropyLoss NaN on Pure Ignore-Index Batch Loss Training occasionally outputs a single `nan` loss on specific batches, often highly padded batches or fully masked out labels. Subsequent training continues, but if gradients are unscaled and stepped, weights become corrupted. Empty Batch Division Loss equals exactly nan RuntimeError: unscale_() expected input to not be nan When using `torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss(ignore_index=-100, reduction='mean')`, if every target in the batch happens to equal `-100`, PyTorch calculates the sum of the valid losses (which is 0) and divides by the number of valid targets (which is also 0). This results in 0/0, which is NaN.

encyclopedia.text: RMSNorm Variance Overflow in FP16 Model Model loss becomes NaN almost immediately at the start of training or unexpectedly during training. Activations following the RMSNorm layer are mostly zeros or NaNs. Numerical Instability Loss is NaN at step 0 Gradients containing NaNs in LayerNorm/RMSNorm In RMSNorm, the sum of squared activations is computed. encyclopedia.title: Learned Temperature Collapse in Contrastive Loss
encyclopedia.text: Learned Temperature Collapse in Contrastive Loss Model The contrastive loss initially decreases rapidly but suddenly explodes to NaN. The learned temperature parameter converges towards zero. Loss Divergence Loss drops suddenly, then goes to NaN Gradient norm explodes In contrastive learning (like CLIP), logits are scaled by `1 / temperature`. If the temperature parameter is learned and not constrained, the optimizer may push it towards zero to artificially increase confidence and lower the loss. As temperature approaches 0, logits approach infinity. This causes `CrossEntropyLoss` (which computes exp) to produce infinities, yielding NaNs in the backward pass.

encyclopedia.title: DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 Stale Sync during Grad Clipping
encyclopedia.text: DeepSpeed ZeRO-3 Stale Sync during Grad Clipping Software Training halts abruptly with a deepspeed internal error when calculating the gradient norm for clipping. Only occurs on multi-node setups running ZeRO-3, whereas ZeRO-2 might train perfectly fine. Gradient Explosion AssertionError: Gradient clipping returned NaN DeepSpeed gradient norm is NaN In ZeRO Stage 3, parameters and gradients are partitioned. When computing the global gradient norm for clipping, all ranks must synchronize their local norms. If there is a communication timeout, or if some ranks process empty partitions in a specific mixed-precision context, a rank might send uninitialized or stale gradient buffers containing NaNs. The global all-reduce aggregates these NaNs, causing the entire step to fail.

encyclopedia.title: PyTorch DataLoader Hangs Indefinitely with OpenCV due to Fork
encyclopedia.text: PyTorch DataLoader Hangs Indefinitely with OpenCV due to Fork Software Process hangs indefinitely during enumeration of DataLoader GPU utilization drops to 0% No crash logs or stack traces are emitted DataLoader Deadlock Training freezes at epoch start or mid-epoch No CPU usage, no GPU usage, 0 errors thrown OpenCV's internal multi-threading uses OpenMP/pthreads. When PyTorch DataLoader uses `num_workers > 0` with the `fork` start method, the child processes inherit a corrupted state of locks held by threads in the parent process, leading to a deadlock.

encyclopedia.title: DataLoader Deadlock from Silent Worker OOM
encyclopedia.text: DataLoader Deadlock from Silent Worker OOM Environment Dataloader hangs waiting for data from a worker that no longer exists. Sometimes throws a Bus Error if shared memory (/dev/shm) runs out. Silent hang if Linux OOM killer terminates the child process without the parent receiving the signal correctly in older PyTorch versions. DataLoader Deadlock Bus error (core dumped) RuntimeError: DataLoader worker (pid(s) X) exited unexpectedly When a PyTorch DataLoader worker exceeds available memory (often due to small Docker `/dev/shm`), it is silently killed by the OS OOM killer. The parent process is waiting on a multiprocessing Queue for data from this worker. Because the worker died without sending an EOF or error state, the parent hangs indefinitely.

encyclopedia.title: HDF5 Concurrent Read Deadlock with Multiprocessing
encyclopedia.text: HDF5 Concurrent Read Deadlock with Multiprocessing Data Dataset fails to load intermittently Processes freeze when reading `.h5` files simultaneously in PyTorch dataloader workers Dataset Deadlock HDF5-DIAG: Error detected in HDF5 BlockingIOError: [Errno 11] Resource temporarily unavailable The HDF5 library maintains internal state and file locks. It is not safe to fork a process that has an open HDF5 file handle. When PyTorch creates child workers via fork, they all inherit the same file descriptor and internal HDF5 state, causing corruption or deadlocks when they attempt to read concurrently.

encyclopedia.title: PyTorch Pin_Memory Thread Deadlock
encyclopedia.text: PyTorch Pin_Memory Thread Deadlock Hardware 0% GPU utilization The main thread is blocked waiting for the background `pin_memory` thread. Interrupting the process via Ctrl+C shows it blocked in `queue.get()` from the pin_memory thread. DataLoader Deadlock Training hangs endlessly before moving batch to GPU Stuck at `batch = batch.to(device)` or returning from DataLoader When `pin_memory=True`, PyTorch spawns a background thread to copy pageable host memory to pinned (page-locked) host memory. If the objects returned by the Dataset are not standard tensors (e.g. custom objects, lists of un-pinnable types) or if there's a CUDA driver crash/OOM during the pinning process, the thread dies silently or gets stuck, and the main process hangs forever waiting for the pinned batch.

    return self Teaches the PyTorch pin_memory thread how to properly pin the custom object without crashing/hanging.

encyclopedia.title: TopologyAffinityError Admission Rejection
encyclopedia.text: TopologyAffinityError Admission Rejection Hardware Pod is stuck in a Terminated or Pending state after being scheduled to a node. Deployment fails to scale up despite sufficient total cluster resources. NUMA Scheduling TopologyAffinityError Warning  UnexpectedAdmissionError  <unknown>  kubelet  Update plugin resources failed due to TopologyAffinityError The Kubernetes scheduler is topology-blind. It assigns the Pod to a node based on total available capacity. However, the Kubelet's Topology Manager on the node (often configured with the 'single-numa-node' policy for high-performance GPU workloads) rejects the Pod at admission time because the requested CPU, memory, and GPU resources cannot be satisfied within a single NUMA domain.

encyclopedia.title: Ephemeral Storage Exhaustion by Model Weights
encyclopedia.text: Ephemeral Storage Exhaustion by Model Weights Storage Pod is suddenly evicted with status 'Evicted' during startup or model initialization. The host node transitions into a 'DiskPressure' state. Other random pods on the same node might also be evicted. Node Eviction The node was low on resource: ephemeral-storage. Container <name> was using <size>, which exceeds its request of 0. Machine learning workloads often download massive pre-trained model weights (e.g., from Hugging Face) into the default cache directory (like ~/.cache/huggingface) located on the container's root filesystem. This consumes the node's underlying root partition (ephemeral storage). Without explicit limits, a single pod can fill the disk, triggering a kubelet eviction.

encyclopedia.title: NVIDIA NVML Initialization Failure
encyclopedia.text: NVIDIA NVML Initialization Failure Hardware Pods requesting GPUs are stuck in Pending because the node advertises 0 allocatable GPUs. The NVIDIA device plugin daemonset pod on a specific node is crash-looping. Pods launch but applications immediately crash with 'CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version'. Device Plugin Failed to initialize NVML: Unknown Error Failed to initialize NVML: Driver/library version mismatch The NVIDIA device plugin relies on the NVML library to discover GPUs and report their health to the kubelet. If the underlying GPU hardware experiences a fault (e.g., an Xid error causing it to fall off the PCIe bus), or if there is a cgroup driver mismatch (e.g., systemd vs cgroupfs) breaking container runtime permissions, NVML fails to initialize.

encyclopedia.title: Silent Pod GPU OOM Hang
encyclopedia.text: Silent Pod GPU OOM Hang Memory Application stops processing requests or model training halts indefinitely. Kubernetes reports the Pod status as 'Running' with 0 restarts. Standard resource metrics (CPU/RAM) appear completely normal. Monitoring RuntimeError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate <X> MiB A CUDA Out Of Memory (OOM) error is an application-level exception thrown by the CUDA runtime to the framework (e.g., PyTorch). Unlike a system RAM OOM where the Linux kernel's OOM-killer sends a SIGKILL (resulting in an 'OOMKilled' pod state), a CUDA OOM does not automatically terminate the process. If the application catches the exception but fails to exit gracefully, the container remains alive in a deadlocked or idle state.

encyclopedia.title: Time-Slicing Cross-Pod VRAM Exhaustion
encyclopedia.text: Time-Slicing Cross-Pod VRAM Exhaustion Memory A newly scheduled pod immediately crashes with an OOM error upon startup. Existing, previously stable pods suddenly crash with CUDA OOMs at random intervals. Occurs exclusively on nodes where GPU time-slicing (e.g., replicas: 4) is enabled. Isolation CUDA_ERROR_OUT_OF_MEMORY during context initialization Failed to allocate memory for the GPU context Kubernetes GPU time-slicing multiplexes compute execution time, but it provides absolutely zero hardware-level memory isolation. If a physical GPU with 24GB VRAM is time-sliced into 4 logical GPUs, Kubernetes allows scheduling 4 pods to it. If Pod A (the 'noisy neighbor') allocates 20GB of VRAM, Pods B, C, and D will instantly encounter CUDA OOM errors because the physical memory pool is exhausted, despite Kubernetes acting as if they each possess dedicated resources.

encyclopedia.title: Requested node configuration is not available (Memory/CPU Mismatch)
encyclopedia.text: Requested node configuration is not available (Memory/CPU Mismatch) Resource Allocation The job is immediately rejected upon submission via sbatch or salloc. No job ID is returned, and the job never enters the queue. Constraint Mismatch sbatch error: Batch job submission failed: Requested node configuration is not available salloc: error: Requested node configuration is not available The user requested a combination of resources (like --mem-per-cpu combined with a high --ntasks) that exceeds the physical hardware capacity of any single node within the specified partition. Often caused by confusing --mem (total memory per node) with --mem-per-cpu.

encyclopedia.title: Preempted Job Causes Workflow Manager Hard Failure
encyclopedia.text: Preempted Job Causes Workflow Manager Hard Failure Job Execution A long-running machine learning job is killed abruptly. The workflow manager (e.g. Nextflow) marks the task as failed and aborts the entire pipeline instead of resubmitting. Preemption Handling slurmstepd: error: *** JOB <ID> ON <node> CANCELLED AT <time> DUE TO PREEMPTION *** Workflow manager error: Job failed with exit code 15 SLURM reclaimed the node for a higher-priority job and sent a SIGTERM. The running application did not catch the signal to gracefully exit or checkpoint within the 2-minute grace period. The workflow manager was not configured to interpret the 'PREEMPTED' (PR) state as a resumable event.

encyclopedia.title: SLURM Requeue Fails on Preemption in Cloud Environments
encyclopedia.text: SLURM Requeue Fails on Preemption in Cloud Environments Job Scheduling Jobs submitted with `#SBATCH --requeue` are fully canceled when preempted instead of going back into the queue. Compute node is lost abruptly. Requeue Configuration Job state changes to CANCELLED instead of PENDING after preemption scontrol: error: requeue failed In elastic cloud clusters (like AWS Spot instances), the compute node itself may be terminated by the cloud provider before SLURM's slurmctld can successfully execute the requeue command. Alternatively, `JobRequeue=1` is not set in `slurm.conf`.

encyclopedia.title: Atomic Save I/O Error on Parallel FS
encyclopedia.text: Atomic Save I/O Error on Parallel FS Storage Checkpoint saving fails intermittently with I/O errors Training crashes during atomic rename of checkpoint files Lustre File System OSError: [Errno 5] Input/output error OSError: [Errno 116] Stale file handle PyTorch Lightning uses atomic saves by default, saving to a temporary directory (`/tmp`) and then renaming. If `/tmp` is on a different filesystem than the destination (Lustre), the rename triggers a cross-device move or heavy metadata load, causing Lustre to throttle or error out.

encyclopedia.title: NCCL Timeout During Synchronous Checkpoint Save
encyclopedia.text: NCCL Timeout During Synchronous Checkpoint Save Network Training hangs or crashes precisely when saving a checkpoint Rank 0 is busy writing to storage while other ranks timeout waiting for the next collective operation NCCL Timeout RuntimeError: NCCL error: unhandled system error Watchdog caught collective operation timeout ncclCommWatchdogThread: timeout Synchronous checkpointing blocks the training loop. On slow shared storage (e.g., NFS), Rank 0 takes a long time to write the file. Meanwhile, other ranks reach the next distributed collective (e.g., all-reduce) and wait. If the wait exceeds the NCCL timeout (default 30 mins), the watchdog kills the process.

encyclopedia.title: FSDP Checkpoint S3 Path Malformation
encyclopedia.text: FSDP Checkpoint S3 Path Malformation Storage FSDP distributed checkpointing fails when saving directly to an S3 URI Checkpoints are not found when attempting to resume S3 Path Resolution FileNotFoundError: s3:/bucket/path ValueError: Invalid S3 URI FSDP checkpointing often relies on utilities like `pathlib.Path` which are designed for local filesystems. encyclopedia.title: PyTorch vs System CUDA Compilation Mismatch
encyclopedia.text: PyTorch vs System CUDA Compilation Mismatch Environment Installation of flash-attn from source fails during the build step. Pip installation aborts with a RuntimeError mentioning CUDA version mismatch. Dependency Version Mismatch RuntimeError: The detected CUDA version (.*) mismatches the version that was used to compile PyTorch (.*) RuntimeError: nvcc mismatch FlashAttention compiles custom CUDA kernels during installation via `setup.py`. It queries PyTorch for its compiled CUDA version (`torch.version.cuda`) and compares it against the system's `nvcc` compiler version. If they do not match exactly, the build script intentionally raises an error to prevent generating incompatible binaries that would segfault at runtime.

encyclopedia.title: Pre-built Wheel Undefined Symbol Error
encyclopedia.text: Pre-built Wheel Undefined Symbol Error Environment FlashAttention installs successfully via pip using a pre-compiled wheel. Importing flash_attn in Python immediately crashes with an `ImportError` regarding undefined symbols. ABI Incompatibility ImportError: .*undefined symbol: _ZN2at4_ops19empty_memory_format4callEN3c108ArrayRefIlEENS2_8optionalINS2_10ScalarTypeEEENS5_INS2_6LayoutEEENS5_INS2_6DeviceEEENS5_IbEENS5_INS2_12MemoryFormatEEE ImportError: cannot import name 'flash_attn_2_cuda' from 'flash_attn' The user installed a pre-built wheel of `flash-attn` compiled against a specific PyTorch and CUDA version (e.g., PyTorch 2.1.0 + cu118), but their runtime environment has a different PyTorch version (e.g., PyTorch 2.2.0 + cu121). C++ extensions in PyTorch are tightly coupled to the PyTorch ABI (Application Binary Interface). Mismatched PyTorch versions lead to unresolved symbols at load time.

encyclopedia.title: FlashAttention Unsupported GPU Architecture
encyclopedia.text: FlashAttention Unsupported GPU Architecture Hardware Code runs fine on a modern GPU (like A100 or RTX 3090) but crashes when migrated to an older GPU (like V100 or T4). Architecture Mismatch RuntimeError: FlashAttention only supports Ampere GPUs or newer. NotImplementedError: FlashAttention is not supported for this GPU architecture. FlashAttention v2 heavily optimizes memory access and matrix multiplication using specific hardware features introduced in NVIDIA's Ampere architecture (Compute Capability 8.0+), such as asynchronous memory copies and specific Tensor Core instructions. Older architectures (Volta, Turing) lack these hardware features, making the optimized CUDA kernels impossible to run.

encyclopedia.title: PyTorch SDPA FlashAttention Version Incompatibility
encyclopedia.text: PyTorch SDPA FlashAttention Version Incompatibility Software Calling `torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention` is significantly slower than expected. Setting `enable_flash=True` in `sdp_kernel` context manager causes a runtime error or a fallback warning. Feature Deprecation/Version UserWarning: 1Torch was not compiled with flash attention. RuntimeError: No available kernel. Aborting execution. PyTorch introduced `scaled_dot_product_attention` (SDPA) with a built-in FlashAttention backend in version 2.0. However, the specific features supported by the built-in backend depend on the PyTorch version (e.g., PyTorch 2.0 only supports FlashAttention v1, PyTorch 2.2+ integrates FlashAttention v2). If the input tensors require features only available in newer FlashAttention versions (like specific causal masks, sliding window attention, or head dimensions > 64/128), an older PyTorch version will fail to dispatch to the flash backend and silently fallback (or crash if forced).

encyclopedia.title: FlashAttention Build Hang / OOM due to missing Ninja
encyclopedia.text: FlashAttention Build Hang / OOM due to missing Ninja Environment Running `pip install flash-attn` hangs seemingly forever. The build process consumes all system memory and gets killed by the Linux OOM killer. Build System Building wheel for flash-attn (setup.py) ... \n[hangs indefinitely] RuntimeError: ninja is required to build C++ extensions Building FlashAttention requires compiling massive CUDA templates. If the `ninja` build system is not installed, `setuptools` falls back to standard sequential compilation, which takes hours. Furthermore, if `pip` uses build isolation (the default), it creates a temporary environment without the user's installed `ninja` or specific `torch` version, leading to either a missing dependency error, extremely slow builds, or memory exhaustion during compilation.

encyclopedia.action: Install ninja and disable build isolation pip install ninja && pip install --no-build-isolation flash-attn Installing `ninja` enables highly parallel C++ compilation. `--no-build-isolation` forces pip to use the current environment's `torch` and `ninja` instead of building a fresh, isolated one.

encyclopedia.title: Asymmetric Collective Calls leading to NCCL Watchdog Timeout
encyclopedia.text: Asymmetric Collective Calls leading to NCCL Watchdog Timeout Network Training hangs indefinitely without crashing, until the 30-minute NCCL timeout is reached. GPU utilization drops to 0% across all nodes. PyTorch eventually crashes with a watchdog timeout exception. NCCL Timeout RuntimeError: Watchdog caught collective operation timeout: WorkNCCL(SeqNum=... NCCL WARN node [0-9]+ has different rank count Different ranks in the distributed process group execute a different sequence of collective operations (e.g., one rank hits an `if` condition and calls `all_reduce`, while another skips it). Since NCCL relies on matching collective calls across all ranks synchronously, the ranks that called the collective wait forever for the others.
