encyclopedia.title: InfiniBand Link Flap Triggering NCCL Async Handshake Failure
encyclopedia.text: InfiniBand Link Flap Triggering NCCL Async Handshake Failure Hardware Training fails suddenly mid-epoch with a watchdog caught unhandled error. Dmesg on one of the nodes shows InfiniBand link state changing to DOWN then UP. NCCL logs indicate polling failure on completion queue (CQ). Network Partition Watchdog caught unhandled error NCCL WARN Call to ibv_poll_cq failed ib_cq_poll failed: transport retry counter exceeded A brief hardware network event (link flap, switch reset, optical transceiver issue) breaks the reliable InfiniBand (RC) connection between nodes. NCCL encounters an unrecoverable RDMA error and raises it, triggering the PyTorch watchdog to cleanly tear down the job.

encyclopedia.title: GPU Fallen Off Bus (Xid 79) causing Async NCCL Hang
encyclopedia.text: GPU Fallen Off Bus (Xid 79) causing Async NCCL Hang Hardware Distributed training halts. One process reports a CUDA unhandled system error, while others hit NCCL timeout. Running `nvidia-smi` on the affected node hangs or shows missing GPUs. Xid Error CUDA error: unhandled system error RuntimeError: NCCL error in: ... unhandled system error NVRM: Xid (PCI:[0-9a-f:]+): 79, GPU has fallen off the bus. A severe hardware fault (often power delivery or PCIe signal integrity) causes the GPU to disconnect from the PCIe bus entirely. The CUDA runtime loses contact with the device, and NCCL operations immediately fail, cascading into timeouts across other nodes waiting for this GPU.

encyclopedia.title: FSDP Mismatched Tensor Shapes Triggering NCCL Hang
encyclopedia.text: FSDP Mismatched Tensor Shapes Triggering NCCL Hang Model Training hangs specifically during the backward pass or optimizer step when using Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP). The hang occurs reliably at the same point (e.g., first iteration of an epoch where variable sequence length is introduced). NCCL Timeout Watchdog caught collective operation timeout: WorkNCCL(SeqNum=..., OpType=ALLGATHER RuntimeError: NCCL error in: /pytorch/torch/lib/c10d/ProcessGroupNCCL.cpp In FSDP, dynamic input shapes or uneven batch sizes across ranks can lead to mismatched tensor sizes during the AllGather operation for gradients or model parameters. NCCL expects the collective operation to use exact matching sizes across all ranks; otherwise, it hangs waiting for the expected byte count.

encyclopedia.title: Fabric-Induced SM Containment Cascade
encyclopedia.text: Fabric-Induced SM Containment Cascade Hardware NVRM: Xid (PCI:0000:XX:00): 94, pid=XXXX, Contained: SM (0x1). RST: No, D-RST: No XID 137 (NVLink TLC RX PRIV Error) XID 74(NVLINK Error) detected pcie/nvlink user-report Multiple GPUs across different physical nodes simultaneously throw Xid 94. encyclopedia.title: PDN Resonance-Induced Silent Data Corruption
encyclopedia.text: PDN Resonance-Induced Silent Data Corruption Hardware No system or kernel logs generated. Loss spikes, NaN generation, or checkpoint divergence. power delivery user-report The training loss diverges inexplicably despite a stable learning rate. The model begins generating gibberish or NaN values. Hardware logs (dmesg, Xid, DCGM) appear completely healthy with 0 errors. Highly synchronous computational workloads (like dense GEMMs in LLMs) cause periodic power oscillations that resonate with the physical PDN, causing voltage droops that violate logic gate timing margins.

encyclopedia.title: Root FSDP Activation Checkpointing Backward Assert
encyclopedia.text: Root FSDP Activation Checkpointing Backward Assert Model AssertionError: APIs are called in the incorrect state trigger an assert on the backward pass fsdp user-report The forward pass completes successfully. The application crashes immediately upon calling `loss.backward()`. The error only surfaces when activation checkpointing is explicitly enabled alongside FSDP. Nesting all parameters deep within child FSDP modules leaves the outer FSDP root empty. When activation checkpointing triggers recomputation, the lack of parameters in the root module desynchronizes the FSDP state machine during the backward hooks.

encyclopedia.title: vLLM refuses to start with No available memory for the cache blocks
encyclopedia.text: vLLM refuses to start with No available memory for the cache blocks Memory ValueError: No available memory for the cache blocks. Try increasing `gpu_memory_utilization` when initializing the engine. Traceback runs through vllm/v1/engine/core.py, _initialize_kv_caches, get_kv_cache_configs and check_enough_kv_cache_memory Free memory on device reported as lower than the desired utilization target Raising gpu_memory_utilization by a few hundredths flips the failure to CUDA out of memory instead, with no value that works in between vllm kv-cache gpu-memory-utilization inference-serving startup-failure paged-attention vLLM exits at startup instead of serving, before any request is accepted nvidia-smi shows several gigabytes still free on the card while vLLM reports it has no memory Lowering gpu_memory_utilization makes the error appear sooner rather than fixing it A second model launched onto a GPU that already hosts one fails while the first succeeded vLLM does not allocate whatever memory happens to be free. It fixes a budget of gpu_memory_utilization multiplied by TOTAL device memory, then subtracts model weights, the profiled activation peak and CUDA graph memory. Whatever remains becomes the paged KV cache. The error means weights plus activations already met or exceeded that budget, so the remainder was zero or too small for one block. Because the budget is a fraction of total rather than of free memory, memory held by any other process on the same device is inside the fraction vLLM believes it owns but cannot actually use. Co-locating a second engine is the common form: the second engine profiles against a GPU the first has already filled, so its fraction has to cover both footprints. The counterintuitive consequence is that seeing this error alongside plenty of idle VRAM usually means the budget is too SMALL, not too large. Instinct trained on out-of-memory errors says lower the number, and lowering it makes this failure worse.

encyclopedia.action: Raise --gpu-memory-utilization toward 0.90 to 0.95 when the GPU is otherwise idle. This is what the error message itself advises and it is correct for the single-tenant case.
steps: Raise --gpu-memory-utilization toward 0.90 to 0.95 when the GPU is otherwise idle. This is what the error message itself advises and it is correct for the single-tenant case.
Lower --max-model-len. The activation peak vLLM profiles scales with sequence length, so a shorter served context returns budget to the cache.
Reduce --max-num-seqs and --max-num-batched-tokens to cut the profiled peak without changing the served context length.
Add --enforce-eager to reclaim the memory reserved for CUDA graphs. This is not always sufficient on its own.
When sharing one GPU between engines, size each fraction to cover the co-tenant. Two engines at 0.5 and 0.45 of total memory do not fit, because each fraction is measured against the whole card.

encyclopedia.title: vLLM rejects a request because the prompt plus completion exceeds the served context length
encyclopedia.text: vLLM rejects a request because the prompt plus completion exceeds the served context length Memory ValueError: This model's maximum context length is 4096 tokens, however you requested 5120 tokens. Reduce max_model_len or the prompt length. The model's max seq len is larger than the maximum number of tokens that can be stored in KV cache. Try increasing gpu_memory_utilization or decreasing max_model_len when initializing the engine. A served context length that matches max_position_embeddings in the model config rather than the length the model card advertises vllm max-model-len context-length inference-serving max-position-embeddings request-rejection A request is rejected although the model card advertises a much longer context The same prompt succeeds against a different deployment of the same model Shortening the prompt clears the error even though the completion length was never changed Raising the served context length triggers a different startup error about KV cache capacity The limit is applied to prompt tokens plus requested completion tokens, not to the prompt alone. A prompt that fits on its own still fails when max_tokens is added to it, which is why reducing the requested completion sometimes clears the error without touching the input. vLLM derives the served window from the model configuration, reading max_position_embeddings. A repository whose card advertises a long context while its config.json declares a shorter max_position_embeddings will serve the shorter one, and the error names that shorter number. The served window can also be capped below the configured one at startup when the KV cache cannot hold the full length within the memory budget. In that case the engine logs the cap and every later request is judged against the reduced number.

encyclopedia.action: Set --max-model-len explicitly at launch to the length you intend to serve, rather than relying on the value inferred from the model config.
steps: Set --max-model-len explicitly at launch to the length you intend to serve, rather than relying on the value inferred from the model config.
Derive max_tokens on the client from the remaining budget instead of hardcoding it, so prompt plus completion cannot exceed the window.

Inspect max_position_embeddings in the model's config.json before assuming the advertised context is what will be served, and override with --hf-overrides or an explicit --max-model-len where the config is wrong.

If raising --max-model-len produces the KV cache capacity error at startup, raise --gpu-memory-utilization, quantize the KV cache, or add tensor parallelism, because the memory rather than the model is now the limit.
Chunk the input on the client where the workload genuinely exceeds the window; splitting the request is the only fix that does not trade away memory elsewhere.

encyclopedia.title: trtllm-build fails because an optimization profile has a minimum dimension above its optimum
encyclopedia.text: trtllm-build fails because an optimization profile has a minimum dimension above its optimum Environment [TRT-LLM] [E] Error building engine: optimization profile is invalid. min dimension is greater than opt dimension for input_ids Build aborts during profile validation, before any TensorRT kernel timing begins tensorrt-llm trtllm-build optimization-profile engine-build opt-num-tokens inference-build trtllm-build aborts before an engine file is produced The same flags built successfully against an earlier TensorRT-LLM version The failing dimension is not named in the default build output, so there is nothing to correct Removing one flag makes the build succeed without explaining which value was inconsistent TensorRT validates each optimization profile by checking that the maximum dimensions are at least the optimum, and the optimum at least the minimum. TensorRT-LLM runs the same check earlier, during its own pre-build pass, so that the message names the failure rather than surfacing a raw TensorRT assertion. The usual trigger is opt_num_tokens sitting below the minimum implied by other flags. It defaults to max_batch_size multiplied by max_beam_width, so setting it by hand while leaving those flags to grow can place opt underneath the derived min for a batched dimension such as input_ids. With --multiple_profiles the profile-splitting logic generates several min, opt and max tuples rather than one. A value that is consistent in the first profile can be inconsistent in another, which is why the build can fail while the flags look reasonable.

encyclopedia.action: Re-run the build with TLLM_LOG_LEVEL=TRACE, which prints a table of every input tensor with its minimum, optimum and maximum columns. Find the row where the minimum exceeds the optimum; that names the dimension to correct.
steps: Re-run the build with TLLM_LOG_LEVEL=TRACE, which prints a table of every input tensor with its minimum, optimum and maximum columns. Find the row where the minimum exceeds the optimum; that names the dimension to correct.
Remove --opt_num_tokens and let it default to max_batch_size multiplied by max_beam_width, then reintroduce it only if profiling shows a benefit.

Check that max_input_len is less than or equal to max_seq_len, and that max_num_tokens is at least max_batch_size. Note that max_seq_len is deduced from the model config when unspecified, so an automatic value can contradict a flag you set by hand.

Disable --multiple_profiles to confirm whether profile generation rather than a single flag is producing the invalid tuple. If the build then succeeds, reintroduce it after the underlying value is fixed.

encyclopedia.title: TensorRT-LLM rejects FP8 quantization on a GPU below compute capability 8.9
encyclopedia.text: TensorRT-LLM rejects FP8 quantization on a GPU below compute capability 8.9 Environment [TRT-LLM] [E] FP8 quantization is not supported on this GPU architecture (compute capability 8.0). Rebuild the engine with a supported quantization mode. Build aborts during quantization setup rather than at inference time nvidia-smi reports an A100, A30 or another Ampere part while the build requests an FP8 mode tensorrt-llm fp8 quantization compute-capability ampere engine-build inference-build The engine build fails immediately on an A100 while the same command succeeds on an H100 A blog post or vendor page claims the GPU is supported, contradicting the build result Cross-compiling on an Ampere host for a Hopper target fails even though the target would support FP8 It is unclear which quantization to use instead without losing the memory saving that motivated FP8 NVIDIA documents FP8 support as requiring compute capability greater than 8.9, which covers Ada, Hopper, Blackwell and later. Ampere reports 8.0 and has no FP8 tensor cores, so there is no kernel for TensorRT-LLM to select and the constraint cannot be worked around by a flag. The check is enforced when the engine is built, not when it is loaded. Building on an Ampere host for an Ada or Hopper target therefore fails as well, unless an explicitly supported cross-compilation flow is used. Third-party guides that list the A100 as FP8-capable, sometimes citing a strongly typed build flag, contradict both NVIDIA's documentation and the hardware. Treat the vendor documentation as authoritative here.

encyclopedia.action: On compute capability 8.0 or below, build with INT8 SmoothQuant or INT4 AWQ instead. Both run on Ampere and recover most of the throughput and memory benefit that motivated FP8.
steps: On compute capability 8.0 or below, build with INT8 SmoothQuant or INT4 AWQ instead. Both run on Ampere and recover most of the throughput and memory benefit that motivated FP8.
Where accuracy matters more than footprint, build in FP16 or BF16 and recover memory through batching and KV cache settings rather than through weight quantization.
For KV cache savings specifically, use the INT8 KV cache path on Ampere. The FP8 KV cache is preferred on Ada and Hopper for its smaller accuracy impact, but it is not available below 8.9.
Run the build on a machine whose GPU matches the deployment target, or use a documented cross-compilation flow, because the architecture check happens at build time.
Confirm the target's compute capability before selecting a quantization mode rather than inferring it from the product name.

encyclopedia.title: vLLM returns 500 on every request after the EngineCore process dies
encyclopedia.text: vLLM returns 500 on every request after the EngineCore process dies Reliability vllm.v1.engine.exceptions.EngineDeadError: EngineCore encountered an issue. See stack trace (above) for the root cause. Engine core proc EngineCore_DP0 died unexpectedly, shutting down client Traceback through output_handler, await engine_core.get_output_async, core_client.py get_output_async AsyncEngineDeadError: Background loop has errored already on the older V0 engine POST /v1/chat/completions HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error repeating for every subsequent request vllm enginedeaderror engine-core inference-serving outage v1-engine Every completion request returns HTTP 500 while the container stays up and the port stays open A liveness probe that only checks the port keeps the dead instance in the load balancer The error the server reports names no cause, so there is nothing obvious to act on Restarting clears it for a while and it returns under the same conditions EngineDeadError is a bereavement notice, not a diagnosis. The API server process discovers the child is gone when it next awaits output, and reports that discovery. The exception that actually killed the engine was raised inside the EngineCore subprocess and printed to its own stream earlier, which is what the message means by see stack trace above. The child dies for reasons that share nothing but their effect. Reported causes include kernels that do not exist for the device, where a quantized build raises CUDA error no kernel image is available for execution on the device on the first request; an execute_model remote call timing out against a stalled worker; the kernel out-of-memory killer reaping the subprocess under load; and shared-memory limits breaking worker startup. The failure is durable because nothing restarts the engine. The parent has no model of its own to fall back on, so it stays alive serving errors, and a port-based liveness probe cannot tell that apart from a working server.

encyclopedia.action: Scroll back in the logs to the first traceback printed by the EngineCore or worker process. That is the diagnosable error; the EngineDeadError below it is only the parent noticing.

If the engine died on the very first request rather than under load, suspect kernel support for the device before suspecting memory, and confirm the quantization format is built for the target compute capability.
Check dmesg and nvidia-smi for an out-of-memory kill or an Xid entry. A subprocess reaped by the kernel leaves no Python traceback at all, which is the case most often misread as a vLLM bug.
Re-run with VLLM_LOGGING_LEVEL=DEBUG and --enforce-eager. Eager mode removes CUDA graph capture from the set of possible causes in one step.
Raise the container shared-memory limit or run with host IPC when the failure appears during worker startup under tensor parallelism.

encyclopedia.title: vLLM throughput collapses as the scheduler preempts and recomputes the same requests
encyclopedia.text: vLLM throughput collapses as the scheduler preempts and recomputes the same requests Performance Sequence group 0 is preempted by PreemptionMode.RECOMPUTE mode because there is not enough KV cache space. The same warning repeating continuously rather than appearing in occasional bursts A steadily climbing vllm:num_preemptions_total in the Prometheus metrics total_cumulative_preemption_cnt rising in the periodic stats line vllm preemption recompute kv-cache scheduler throughput serving-performance Throughput falls sharply while GPU utilisation stays high, so the card looks busy and productive Latency becomes erratic, with individual requests taking many times their usual time Nothing errors, so no alert fires and no exception appears in the logs Adding load makes total completed requests go down rather than up Preemption is a safety valve that keeps the server up when the cache cannot hold every batched request. It is not free: an evicted sequence loses the decode work it had already done and is prefilled again from the beginning when it is re-admitted. That makes the failure self-sustaining. Re-admitted sequences need cache and compute to redo their prefill, which is exactly the pressure that caused the eviction, so the scheduler evicts again. Once the loop closes, a growing fraction of each step is spent recomputing rather than retiring requests, and the fleet does less work the more traffic it is given. It is easy to miss because nothing fails. There is no exception and no error rate to alert on; the only signals are a warning line and a counter, and utilisation stays high throughout because the GPU is genuinely busy doing the wasted work.

encyclopedia.action: Lower --max-num-seqs so the scheduler admits fewer concurrent sequences than the cache can hold. Capping admission is the direct fix for a thrashing loop, because it stops the condition rather than enlarging the resource.
steps: Lower --max-num-seqs so the scheduler admits fewer concurrent sequences than the cache can hold. Capping admission is the direct fix for a thrashing loop, because it stops the condition rather than enlarging the resource.
Set --max-model-len to the length the workload actually needs rather than the model's full context window. Every admitted sequence reserves capacity for its full declared length.

Raise --gpu-memory-utilization to enlarge the cache, but do so incrementally and validate at peak load, since taking headroom away from activations and graph buffers can turn preemption warnings into hard failures.
Increase tensor parallel size to spread the cache across more devices when the workload genuinely needs the concurrency.
Quantize the KV cache to roughly double the number of sequences the same memory holds.

encyclopedia.title: vLLM runs out of GPU memory during serving after the prefill token budget is raised
encyclopedia.text: vLLM runs out of GPU memory during serving after the prefill token budget is raised Memory torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory raised during a forward pass while serving rather than during startup Failures beginning immediately after --max-num-batched-tokens or --enable-chunked-prefill was changed A log line advising that if out-of-memory occurs during cudagraph capture, consider decreasing gpu_memory_utilization or switching to eager mode vllm chunked-prefill max-num-batched-tokens cuda-oom throughput-tuning serving-runtime The server starts cleanly and fails only once real traffic arrives The failure correlates with long prompts rather than with the number of concurrent users A configuration tuned for throughput on one model fails on another of similar size Reducing the served context length does not help, because the prompts were already within it Two different budgets draw on the same device memory. gpu_memory_utilization reserves a pool that the KV cache is carved from, while the batched token limit governs how much work a single step may do and therefore how large the activation tensors for that step become. Raising the second does not consult the first. The token budget only binds when a step is large enough to reach it, which requires long prompts or a heavy prefill mix. A deployment can therefore pass startup profiling, serve ordinary traffic for hours, and fail the first time the arriving prompts are long enough to build a full-sized batch. The reason the served context length is not the lever is that the prompts were always inside it. What changed is how many prefill tokens the scheduler is willing to put into one step, which is a throughput setting rather than a capacity one.

encyclopedia.action: Lower --max-num-batched-tokens toward 2048 to 4096 as the first move when the failure appears at runtime rather than at startup. This is the setting that grew the step.
steps: Lower --max-num-batched-tokens toward 2048 to 4096 as the first move when the failure appears at runtime rather than at startup. This is the setting that grew the step.
Reduce --max-num-seqs next, to 256 or 128 for large models or long-context work, which lowers how many sequences can contribute to a single batch.
Adjust --gpu-memory-utilization only after those two, and do not exceed roughly 0.95, since vLLM needs headroom for activations and the CUDA context.
Add --enforce-eager if the failure occurs during graph capture, which removes the memory reserved for CUDA graphs.

Tune by measurement rather than by arithmetic: raise the budget until the deployment fails at representative load, then step back one notch and keep that value with the model and hardware recorded next to it.

encyclopedia.title: vLLM tensor parallelism fails in a container because shared memory is limited to 64 MB
encyclopedia.text: vLLM tensor parallelism fails in a container because shared memory is limited to 64 MB Infrastructure torch.distributed.DistBackendError: NCCL error, unhandled system error, ncclSystemError NCCL WARN Error while creating shared memory segment /dev/shm/nccl-vzIpS6 A warning that the object store is using /tmp instead of /dev/shm because /dev/shm has only 67108864 bytes available, which will harm performance Initialisation hanging at ncclCommInitRank with no further output vllm tensor-parallel shared-memory docker nccl kubernetes ipc The same image and model work with one GPU and fail with two or more The failure occurs during initialisation, before any request is served The error names NCCL or a shared memory segment, which does not obviously implicate the container runtime The deployment works locally and fails on the orchestrator, or the reverse Container runtimes mount a small tmpfs at /dev/shm by default, historically 64 MB. That default was chosen for ordinary applications and is unrelated to what collective communication libraries need. Tensor-parallel vLLM moves tensors between worker processes through that space, and NCCL creates segments there during communicator setup. When the mount is too small the segment cannot be created and initialisation fails with a system error that names the segment rather than the limit, which is why the cause is not obvious from the message. The failure is invisible on a single GPU because nothing needs the shared segment. It appears the first time the deployment is scaled across devices, which is often long after the image was validated.

encyclopedia.action: Start the container with a larger shared memory allocation, for example a size of 16 GB, or grant it access to the host's shared memory with the host IPC option.
steps: Start the container with a larger shared memory allocation, for example a size of 16 GB, or grant it access to the host's shared memory with the host IPC option.
On Kubernetes, mount an emptyDir with the memory medium and an explicit size limit at /dev/shm, since the pod default is generally insufficient.
On Docker Swarm, use the shared memory size setting rather than host IPC, because Swarm does not support the host IPC option.
Add the IPC_LOCK capability where GPUDirect RDMA is in use, which vLLM's troubleshooting guide names alongside an unmounted shared memory directory as a cause of communicator initialisation failure.

If the failure persists with a large and demonstrably free shared memory mount, suspect segment cleanup rather than size: setting RemoveIPC to no in the logind configuration stops systemd deleting segments that are still in use.

encyclopedia.title: vLLM workers time out reading the shared-memory broadcast ring and the engine dies
encyclopedia.text: vLLM workers time out reading the shared-memory broadcast ring and the engine dies Communication File vllm/distributed/device_communicators/shm_broadcast.py, line 443, in acquire_read raise TimeoutError TimeoutError with no message, followed by The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception An RPC call to execute_model timed out immediately before the engine reports it has died The step timed out waiting on the shared-memory ring buffer, so the engine stalled rather than erroring in the worker The engine hangs at the fan-out: workers show no progress and the reader is still waiting when the deadline passes A stalled step is indistinguishable from a dead worker, so the deadlock surfaces as a bare TimeoutError Environment lines showing NCCL_CUMEM_ENABLE=0 and TORCHINDUCTOR_COMPILE_THREADS=1 captured alongside the traceback vllm shm-broadcast timeouterror execute_model worker-rpc tensor-parallel The traceback names a contextlib helper and a ring-buffer read rather than any model code The exception carries no message at all, so there is nothing in it to search for It appears under load or on long steps and cannot be reproduced with a single short request Raising the engine iteration timeout postpones the failure without changing anything The ring buffer read is bounded by a deadline, not by liveness. The reader cannot distinguish a worker that has crashed from one that is merely slow, so both produce the same bare TimeoutError, and the exception is raised at the point of waiting rather than at the point of trouble. That is why the traceback is so unhelpful: the frames belong to the transport that noticed, and the worker that caused it is a different process which may still be running and may have printed nothing. The failure surfaces at the boundary between processes, which is the one place with no information about either side. Because the deadline is fixed while step duration is not, anything that lengthens a step pushes it toward the limit. A step that takes longer than the reader will wait is indistinguishable from a dead worker, so a purely performance problem is delivered as a fatal transport error.

encyclopedia.action: Establish first whether the worker died or merely ran late. A worker process still alive in the process table after the timeout means the step was slow, not lost, and the remedy is to shorten steps rather than to harden the transport.
steps: Establish first whether the worker died or merely ran late. A worker process still alive in the process table after the timeout means the step was slow, not lost, and the remedy is to shorten steps rather than to harden the transport.
Shorten the step by lowering the batched token budget and the number of concurrent sequences, which reduces the time a single fan-out has to complete in.
Remove one-off delays from the measured path by warming compilation before serving traffic, since a first step that compiles can exceed a deadline that every later step meets comfortably.
Check that no other tenant is contending for the shared memory mount, because a slow ring buffer read is as fatal here as a slow worker.
Treat a raised engine iteration timeout as a diagnostic that buys time to observe, not as a fix; it changes when the failure occurs and not whether the step fits.

encyclopedia.title: vLLM crashes initialising an NVFP4 model because the emulation lookup table stays on the CPU
encyclopedia.text: vLLM crashes initialising an NVFP4 model because the emulation lookup table stays on the CPU Environment RuntimeError: indices should be either on cpu or on the same device as the indexed tensor (cpu) Traceback ending in nvfp4_emulation_utils.py, in break_fp4_bytes A log line stating that the EMULATION NvFp4 MoE backend was selected out of the potential backends The crash occurring during engine init, before any generation vllm nvfp4 quantization emulation device-mismatch modelopt engine-init The model loads and then the engine dies during initialisation rather than during generation The same checkpoint is reported working elsewhere, on hardware with a real NVFP4 backend The error names an indexing rule rather than the quantization format, so the connection is not obvious Nothing in the launch command mentions emulation, which was selected automatically PyTorch requires the index tensor and the tensor being indexed to live on one device, or the index to be on the CPU. The emulation helper builds its constant table as a plain tensor, which lands on the CPU, and then indexes it with values that have already been moved to the accelerator, so the pair straddles the boundary the rule forbids. The path is only reached when backend selection has exhausted every accelerated option. That makes the failure look hardware-specific when it is really a fallback that few deployments exercise, which is why the same checkpoint is reported working on machines that never enter emulation. It fires during initialisation because the unpacking happens while weights are being prepared rather than while tokens are being produced, so there is no partially working server to inspect.

encyclopedia.action: Check which backend was chosen. The log states the selected NvFp4 backend and lists the alternatives, and emulation appearing there is the signal that no accelerated path was available.
steps: Check which backend was chosen. The log states the selected NvFp4 backend and lists the alternatives, and emulation appearing there is the signal that no accelerated path was available.
Remove whatever excluded the faster backends. Batch-invariant mode is the common cause, and clearing it restores selection of an accelerated backend that never touches the emulated helper.
Install or enable a build providing a real NVFP4 backend for the target device, since emulation exists as a correctness fallback rather than as a serving path.
Serve a checkpoint quantized to a format the deployment has hardware support for when no NVFP4 backend can be provided, rather than relying on emulation to bridge the gap.

encyclopedia.title: TensorRT-LLM fails at model init because the FlashInfer FMHA kernel has no build for the GPU architecture
encyclopedia.text: TensorRT-LLM fails at model init because the FlashInfer FMHA kernel has no build for the GPU architecture Environment RuntimeError: Error in function 'TllmGenFmhaRunner' at flashinfer/trtllm/fmha/fmhaRunner.cuh: Unsupported architecture Failure occurring after a model init total timing line, not during weight download The same checkpoint serving normally on a different GPU generation with an unchanged command Quantization configuration naming NVFP4 with modelopt as the producer tensorrt-llm flashinfer fmha unsupported-architecture sm120 blackwell trtllm-serve The container release is current and the model is supported, yet initialisation fails on this card The error is raised from a FlashInfer header path, which does not appear in the TensorRT-LLM command that was run Both a small inference card and a new flagship can hit it, which makes the pattern look inconsistent Model loading reports success first, so the failure looks like a serving problem rather than a support one Fused attention is not written per model; it is a prebuilt kernel selected at runtime. The build carries object code for an enumerated list of architectures, and a device outside that list has nothing to dispatch to, so the runner refuses rather than falling back. The list is a property of the bundled FlashInfer build rather than of TensorRT-LLM or of the checkpoint, which is why the error names a header inside FlashInfer and why nothing in the invocation hints at it. Coverage is not monotonic with newness. Hardware released after the image predates nothing it can use, and modest inference parts are sometimes left out of a build aimed at data-centre silicon, so both the newest and the smallest devices fail while the middle of the range works.

encyclopedia.action: Read the compute capability of the target device and compare it against the architectures the bundled kernel was built for, rather than assuming a current release covers current hardware.
steps: Read the compute capability of the target device and compare it against the architectures the bundled kernel was built for, rather than assuming a current release covers current hardware.

Move to a container build whose kernels enumerate the device. For newly released silicon this usually means a later image; the fix is a build with the architecture compiled in, not a configuration change.
Select an attention backend that does have a build for the device where the framework allows one, since the rejection comes from one kernel provider rather than from attention as a whole.
Where neither is available, serve the model on a GPU generation the image covers and treat the unsupported device as unsupported rather than as misconfigured.

encyclopedia.title: TensorRT-LLM refuses a quantized checkpoint because its weight mapper does not recognise the export layout
encyclopedia.text: TensorRT-LLM refuses a quantized checkpoint because its weight mapper does not recognise the export layout Data Integrity AssertionError: Expected packed qkv scale tensor with leading dim 64, got torch.Size([8192, 20]) assert tensor.shape[0] == expected_total_blocks raised in _split_qkv_scale_tensor Traceback ending in tensorrt_llm/_torch/models/checkpoints/hf/qwen3_5_weight_mapper.py Checkpoint load aborts inside the architecture weight mapper before any engine build begins A weight mapper rejecting ModelOpt W4A16_AWQ checkpoints during load Errors naming a model-specific weight mapper rather than a file or a checksum Failure occurring at load time, before any engine build or serving begins The unquantized variant of the same model loading without error tensorrt-llm modelopt awq w4a16 weight-mapper checkpoint load packed qkv scale tensor quantization A checkpoint that other tools load without complaint is refused here The rejection names a mapper or a key rather than saying what layout was expected Re-exporting with different settings sometimes works, without making clear which setting mattered The same model in an unquantized form loads normally Loading is a translation step, not a copy. Each supported architecture has a mapper that knows which exported tensor becomes which internal parameter, including how quantized weights, scales and zero points are grouped. That knowledge is written per scheme, so a scheme it was not written for has no route through. Quantized exports carry additional tensors that unquantized ones do not, and their names differ between producers and between versions of one producer. The mapper is therefore coupled to the exporting tool in a way the checkpoint format alone does not express, which is why a file can be internally consistent and still unloadable. The rejection is not evidence of corruption. Nothing about the bytes is wrong; the reader simply has no rule for the layout it found, which is why other tools accept the identical file.

encyclopedia.action: Establish first that the file is intact by loading it with the tool that produced it. A successful load there rules out corruption and localises the problem to the mapper.
steps: Establish first that the file is intact by loading it with the tool that produced it. A successful load there rules out corruption and localises the problem to the mapper.
Match the quantizer version to the TensorRT-LLM version rather than treating them as independent, since the naming a mapper expects is set by the producer it was written against.
Re-export with the quantization scheme the target release documents as supported for the architecture, rather than the closest neighbouring scheme.
Compare the tensor names in the export against those the mapper expects for the architecture; a systematic prefix or grouping difference identifies the incompatibility precisely.
Where the architecture is genuinely unsupported for the scheme, quantize to one it does cover instead of adapting the checkpoint by hand.

encyclopedia.title: TensorRT-LLM serving fails with an AttributeError from the FlashInfer attention backend
encyclopedia.text: TensorRT-LLM serving fails with an AttributeError from the FlashInfer attention backend Environment AttributeError: 'TrtllmAttentionMetadata' object has no attribute 'kv_layout' Traceback ending in tensorrt_llm/_torch/attention_backend/flashinfer.py, in forward_impl, at kv_layout=metadata.kv_layout A log line applying model defaults that select FLASHINFER as the attention backend Warnings about skipping the import of cpp extensions due to an incompatible torch version for torchao tensorrt-llm flashinfer attention-backend kv_layout attributeerror trtllm-serve container-release The failure names an attribute, which reads as a coding error rather than a packaging one The model, the flags and the hardware are all supported, and the command is the documented one It appears in a release-candidate container that is newer than the last one that worked Changing model or batch settings has no effect, because none of them are involved The attention backend and the metadata object it consumes are written in two separately versioned components. The backend reads a field the metadata class in this build never declares, so Python raises at the moment of access. Nothing validates that the two agree before serving begins. Attribute access is late-bound, so the disagreement cannot be detected at import, at model load, or by any flag check. The first request to reach fused attention is where it surfaces, which is why the server starts, reports its defaults, and only then fails. The backend was usually not chosen by the operator. Model defaults applied at load time select it, so the failing component is one the command never mentions and the traceback is the first place it appears.

steps: Read the line reporting which attention backend the applied model defaults selected. It names the component that failed, which the command itself does not.
Move to a container build in which the TensorRT-LLM and FlashInfer versions were released together, rather than upgrading either inside an existing image.
Override the applied default to an attention backend whose interface this build does satisfy, which restores service without waiting for a matched release.
Where the image was modified after publication, rebuild from the published one, since an in-place upgrade of either component is what breaks the pairing.
Treat accompanying warnings about skipped cpp extensions or an incompatible torch version as corroboration that the image's components are mismatched, not as unrelated noise.

encyclopedia.title: An out-of-tree GPU or storage kernel module stops building after a kernel upgrade
encyclopedia.text: An out-of-tree GPU or storage kernel module stops building after a kernel upgrade Infrastructure error: implicit declaration of function, naming a kernel helper the module calls A compiler suggestion of the form did you mean, naming the renamed replacement The installed module version is incompatible with the running kernel version A kernel and module version mismatch, where the module release predates the kernel it is being built against Build output under /var/lib/dkms/<module>/<version>/build/make.log ending at the first such error modprobe reporting that it could not insert the module, or dmesg reporting an unknown symbol GPUDirect, RDMA or a parallel filesystem client silently unavailable after a reboot dkms kernel-module implicit-declaration gpudirect peermem kernel-upgrade incompatible version build-failure A node reboots after routine patching and loses a capability nothing in the change record touched The failure is a compiler error in a log nobody reads, not an alert The module built correctly on this machine last month against the previous kernel Rolling the kernel back restores service, which makes the vendor look blameless and the kernel look at fault The kernel offers no stable internal API. Functions are renamed, moved between headers, or deleted between releases, and out-of-tree code that calls them has to be updated in step. DKMS automates recompilation, not adaptation, so it faithfully rebuilds source that no longer matches the target and reports the mismatch as a compiler error. A missing declaration is fatal rather than a warning because the build treats implicit function declarations as errors. That is deliberate: a silently assumed signature would produce a module that loads and then corrupts memory, which is far worse on a node holding GPU mappings. The blast radius is wider than the module because these components sit under a capability rather than an application. A peer-memory module that fails to build does not announce that GPUDirect is gone; the fabric simply falls back to a slower path, or the mount that needed it is absent, and the first symptom is a performance or availability change nobody connects to a patch.

encyclopedia.action: Read the first error in the module's build log, not the last. The compiler names the exact symbol and usually suggests the replacement, which identifies whether this is a rename, a moved header, or a removal.
steps: Read the first error in the module's build log, not the last. The compiler names the exact symbol and usually suggests the replacement, which identifies whether this is a rename, a moved header, or a removal.
Upgrade the module to a release that declares support for the running kernel. For vendor components this is the intended fix and the only one that survives the next upgrade.

Check the build order where a peer-memory module is involved: the fabric stack must be installed before the GPU driver, because the driver probes for the fabric's symbols while it builds. Reinstalling the GPU driver after the fabric stack resolves the unknown-symbol variant.
Confirm the compiler matches the one the kernel was built with before concluding the source is at fault, since a toolchain mismatch produces an unrelated failure that looks similar.
Where the platform supports it, move to a path that needs no out-of-tree peer-memory module at all, which removes this class of failure rather than deferring it.

encyclopedia.title: TensorRT-LLM conversion and build scripts fail after NumPy is upgraded inside a pinned container
encyclopedia.text: TensorRT-LLM conversion and build scripts fail after NumPy is upgraded inside a pinned container Environment A module that was compiled using NumPy 1.x cannot be run in NumPy 2.x as it may crash Traceback ending in tensorrt_llm/_common.py or tensorrt_llm/builder.py during a conversion or build step TypeError: set_weights_name(): incompatible function arguments. The following argument types are supported Invoked with: an INetworkDefinition, a raw array with a dtype and shape, and a weight name string A pybind11 overload resolution failure where a numpy array is passed where tensorrt.Weights is expected Traceback through tensorrt_llm/parameter.py set_name into network.trt_network.set_weights_name AttributeError or ValueError raised from a compiled extension immediately after import The failure appearing only after a pip install that reported upgrading numpy tensorrt-llm numpy abi container convert-checkpoint dependency-pinning trtllm-build The container is the official one and the command is from the documentation, and it still fails The traceback points into tensorrt_llm rather than at anything that was installed It worked in a fresh container and stopped after an unrelated pip install Reinstalling TensorRT-LLM does not help, because the incompatibility is with a dependency Compiled Python extensions bind to NumPy's binary interface at build time, not at import time. A major NumPy release changes that interface, so an extension built against the previous one is no longer loadable even though the Python-level API looks unchanged and pip records no conflict. The container's value is that its extensions, CUDA libraries and NumPy were built and pinned together. Installing a package whose metadata merely asks for a newer NumPy is enough to break that set, because pip resolves the request without knowing which binaries depend on the version it is replacing. The traceback misleads because the first thing to import a compiled extension is what raises. That is usually a TensorRT-LLM internal module, so the component that reports the failure is rarely the component whose installation caused it.

encyclopedia.action: Pin NumPy back to the major version the image shipped with before doing anything else; the extensions are already built for it and nothing needs recompiling.
steps: Pin NumPy back to the major version the image shipped with before doing anything else; the extensions are already built for it and nothing needs recompiling.
Read the traceback from the bottom upward to the first frame outside NumPy itself. That frame names the package whose binary is incompatible, which is the one to align.
Install model or dataset requirements with the container's pinned versions constrained, so a transitive dependency cannot move a package the image's binaries depend on.
Rebuild the image rather than mutating a running container when a newer NumPy is genuinely required, so the extensions are compiled against the version that will be present.
Prefer the official image for the TensorRT-LLM release in use over assembling the stack by hand, since the pinning is the thing being bought.

encyclopedia.title: DistributedDataParallel raises an internal reducer assertion when a backward pass arrives unexpectedly
encyclopedia.text: DistributedDataParallel raises an internal reducer assertion when a backward pass arrives unexpectedly Distributed Training RuntimeError: expect_autograd_hooks_ INTERNAL ASSERT FAILED at ../torch/csrc/distributed/c10d/reducer.cpp please report a bug to PyTorch appended to the assertion text The failure appearing only when the model is wrapped in DistributedDataParallel Onset coinciding with enabling static_graph or gradient checkpointing rather than with a model change ddp distributeddataparallel reducer static_graph gradient-checkpointing no_sync autograd The error asks you to report a bug to PyTorch, which is almost never the right response The same model trains correctly on a single GPU and only fails once wrapped in DDP It appears after enabling gradient checkpointing or a static graph, neither of which mentions backward counting The traceback points into C++ reducer internals with no application frame to act on The reducer keeps a flag saying a backward pass is expected. DDP sets it when it prepares for backward and clears it when that pass is finalised, and the assertion fires when hooks arrive while the flag is clear. The condition is therefore about counting and ordering, not about the values in any tensor. Static graph tightens the contract: it promises the same graph and exactly one backward per iteration so the reducer can precompute its bucket order. A second backward, or a backward on a second returned tensor, then reaches a reducer that has already finalised and is no longer expecting anything. Gradient checkpointing conflicts by re-running the forward during backward, which can fire the same hooks twice. Its reentrant implementation is the one that does this; the non-reentrant implementation exists partly to be compatible with hook-based systems like DDP. Using no_sync incorrectly desynchronises the same flag. If a forward runs inside the context and its backward outside it, or the reverse, the reducer's expectation and the actual sequence diverge and the assertion is how that divergence surfaces.

encyclopedia.action: Ensure exactly one backward call per DDP forward. Where several losses exist, sum them into one scalar and call backward once rather than backwarding each tensor.
steps: Ensure exactly one backward call per DDP forward. Where several losses exist, sum them into one scalar and call backward once rather than backwarding each tensor.
Turn off static_graph first when diagnosing. It is the strictest contract and the most common thing to have enabled without realising what it promises.
Pass the non-reentrant option to gradient checkpointing, which is the implementation compatible with DDP's hooks, when checkpointing and DDP must be combined.
Keep each forward and its matching backward on the same side of a no_sync context, and check accumulation loops where the boundary can drift by one step.
Where several independent backward passes are genuinely required, run them against the unwrapped module and handle gradient reduction explicitly rather than fighting the reducer.

encyclopedia.title: FSDP2 raises a KeyError on a tied weight while sharding the model
encyclopedia.text: FSDP2 raises a KeyError on a tied weight while sharding the model Distributed Training KeyError: 'lm_head.weight' raised while preparing the model Traceback through accelerator.prepare into _prepare_fsdp2, at a mapping built from old and new named parameters A preceding warning suggesting the config be updated with tie_word_embeddings set to false KeyError reporting that a parameter in the optimizer could not be switched to its sharded version fsdp fsdp2 fully_shard tied-weights lm_head keyerror dtensor The named weight is visibly present in the model, so the error reads as impossible The failure happens during preparation, before any training step The same model trains without complaint under the previous FSDP implementation A warning about weight tying appears above the traceback and is easy to read past Weight tying means two parameter names refer to one tensor object. Code that walks named parameters therefore sees the tensor twice under two names, while code that builds a set or a dict keyed by the tensor sees it once. The mapping from pre-shard to post-shard parameters is built exactly that way, so the second name has no entry and the lookup raises. FSDP2 is more exposed to this than its predecessor because it replaces each parameter with a DTensor carrying its own placement. A tensor shared across two shard groups has no single well-defined placement, so tying is not a cosmetic detail the sharding layer can ignore. The error names the weight rather than the tying, which sends people to look for a missing parameter. Nothing is missing: the name is a second alias for a tensor the mapping already consumed under its first alias.

encyclopedia.action: Disable weight tying in the model configuration and materialise a genuine tensor for the output projection before sharding, which is what the warning above the traceback is telling you to do.
steps: Disable weight tying in the model configuration and materialise a genuine tensor for the output projection before sharding, which is what the warning above the traceback is telling you to do.
Where tying must be preserved, untie before sharding by cloning the embedding tensor into the head, apply sharding, and restore the relationship afterwards.
Pass a non-strict flag when loading a state dictionary into a model whose tied name is absent, then copy the embedding tensor into the tied slot explicitly.
Keep both tied tensors inside the same shard group if the framework allows it, since the ambiguity only arises when one placement has to serve two groups.
Check whether the failure appears on save rather than on prepare; the same missing name breaks optimizer state handling and is fixed the same way.

encyclopedia.title: FSDP preparation fails because activation checkpointing calls a wrapping policy that was never set
encyclopedia.text: FSDP preparation fails because activation checkpointing calls a wrapping policy that was never set Distributed Training TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable raised during model preparation Traceback through accelerator.prepare into the FSDP2 preparation path and an activation-checkpointing helper A configuration selecting no automatic wrapping together with activation checkpointing enabled Could not find the transformer layer class to wrap in the model, when a class name was supplied instead fsdp auto-wrap-policy no-wrap activation-checkpointing typeerror accelerate configuration The error names a type rather than a setting, so it does not point at the configuration that caused it Each of the two options works on its own and only the combination fails The traceback lands in framework internals with no application frame to act on Turning off the wrong one of the two makes it pass and teaches the wrong lesson Selecting no automatic wrapping sets the policy to an empty value, which is correct: there is no policy because nothing is to be wrapped automatically. Activation checkpointing, however, reuses that policy to decide which submodules receive checkpointing, and it assumes something callable is there. The two settings are presented as independent and are not. One expresses an intent about sharding granularity and the other silently consumes it, so a combination the configuration format permits is one the code path cannot serve. A neighbouring failure produces the same empty policy from the other direction: a transformer-based policy on a model that exposes no splittable module list, or with a class name that cannot be resolved, also yields nothing to call.

encyclopedia.action: Choose an explicit wrapping policy and name the layer class to wrap, which gives activation checkpointing something to apply and is the configuration these frameworks are designed around.
steps: Choose an explicit wrapping policy and name the layer class to wrap, which gives activation checkpointing something to apply and is the configuration these frameworks are designed around.
Turn activation checkpointing off if wrapping genuinely must stay manual, since it is the consumer of a policy that no longer exists.
Use a size-based policy with a minimum parameter count where no single layer class is the right unit, which yields a real policy without naming an architecture.
Verify the named layer class actually resolves in the model when a transformer-based policy is selected, because an unresolvable name produces the same empty policy.
Prefer the block that contains attention followed by the feed-forward network as the wrapping unit, and keep weight-sharing submodules inside one unit.

encyclopedia.title: FSDP fails when composed with CPU parameter offloading
encyclopedia.text: FSDP fails when composed with CPU parameter offloading Distributed Training The traceback ending inside HybridDeviceOptimizer while it builds its sub-optimizer parameter groups, not inside the sharding layer A call to param.detach().clone().cpu().pin_memory() applied to a parameter that sharding has already replaced with a DTensor Frames passing through the DTensor dispatcher and its sharding propagator on the way to the failure The failure raised from get_megatron_optimizer during setup_model_and_optimizer, before the first training step Setup or the first training step failing with both sharding and CPU offloading enabled A device or placement error naming a parameter that offloading has moved to host memory The identical configuration succeeding with offloading disabled The identical configuration succeeding with sharding disabled and offloading kept fsdp cpu-offload offloading composition megatron memory-saving Both features are documented and each works by itself The failure appears at setup or on the first step rather than under memory pressure Offloading was enabled precisely because memory was already tight, so simply removing it is not free The error rarely names offloading, so the interaction is not obvious from the message The concrete mechanism in the Megatron implementation is worth stating exactly, because it explains why the error names the optimizer rather than the sharding. The offload path builds its host-side copy by calling detach, clone, cpu and pin_memory on each parameter in turn. Under sharding those parameters are no longer plain tensors but DTensors, so every one of those calls goes through a dispatcher that needs a sharding rule for the operator. Pinning host memory has no meaningful sharded semantics, the rule is absent, and the composition dies in the optimizer constructor. Sharding divides a parameter across ranks and keeps authoritative placement metadata for each piece. Offloading relocates parameters to host memory and restores them on demand, keeping its own view of where each one is. Both are correct in isolation and each expects to be the authority, so composing them leaves two components disagreeing about a single tensor. The disagreement shows up early because placement is resolved during setup and on the first use of a parameter, not when memory runs short. That is why the failure looks unrelated to the memory pressure that motivated enabling offloading. Support for the combination is a property of a specific implementation and version rather than of the idea, so a stack that documents both features separately may not support them together, and a version that works is not evidence a neighbouring one does.

Recover the memory another way when sharding must stay: shard optimizer state and gradients more aggressively, or increase the number of ranks the model is divided across.
Reduce activation memory instead, through checkpointing or a smaller microbatch, since activations are frequently the real pressure and are not what offloading was addressing.
Where the framework supports offloading only at specific granularities, offload the component it names rather than the whole parameter set.
Treat a version that supports the combination as a requirement to pin, because support here moves between releases.

encyclopedia.title: A worker loses its GPU mid-run and the job hangs until a collective times out
encyclopedia.text: A worker loses its GPU mid-run and the job hangs until a collective times out Reliability A fatal timeout arriving several minutes after the last normal progress line RuntimeError reporting a worker failed with a device-lost error from the runtime backend level_zero backend failed with error 20, UR_RESULT_ERROR_DEVICE_LOST on Intel accelerators Xid 79 or a GPU has fallen off the bus message in the host kernel log at the moment progress stopped Peer ranks reporting a collective timeout while the failed rank reports nothing at all device-lost xid-79 hang collective-timeout pipeline-parallel level-zero gpu-fell-off-bus The reported error names a rank that is working correctly, not the one that failed Minutes pass between the real fault and any log line, so the timestamps mislead The job looks alive to the scheduler throughout the stall and keeps its allocation Restarting sometimes works, which suggests a transient software fault rather than hardware A collective is a rendezvous. Every participant blocks until all of them arrive, and there is no mechanism by which a waiting rank learns that a peer has ceased to exist, it can only observe that the data has not come. The absence of a peer and a peer that is merely slow are indistinguishable until a deadline expires. So the failure inverts the usual relationship between cause and report. The rank whose device vanished cannot report anything, because the thing it would report with is gone. The report comes from a healthy rank, describing a symptom of someone else's fault, at a time chosen by the timeout rather than by the event. The device loss itself is a host-level event. It is recorded in the kernel log at the instant it happens, which is why that log and the job's own output disagree about when the failure occurred, often by the whole length of the timeout.

encyclopedia.action: Take the timestamp of the last normal progress line, not the timestamp of the error, and look in the host kernel log of every node at that moment. The device-loss event is recorded there when it happens.
steps: Take the timestamp of the last normal progress line, not the timestamp of the error, and look in the host kernel log of every node at that moment. The device-loss event is recorded there when it happens.
Identify the silent rank rather than the reporting one. The rank that stopped emitting output first is the one whose device went away; the rank in the error message is a witness.
Check the accelerator inventory on each node against what the job expected. A device that has fallen off the bus is frequently absent from the inventory entirely until the host is reset.
Shorten the collective timeout while investigating so the report arrives closer to the event, then restore it, since a short timeout in production converts slow steps into failures.

Drain and test the suspect node rather than restarting the job onto it. A device lost once will usually be lost again, and a restart that lands elsewhere reads as a fix while leaving the fault in the pool.

encyclopedia.title: An inference scheduler deadlocks under sustained load and stops issuing work
encyclopedia.text: An inference scheduler deadlocks under sustained load and stops issuing work Performance assert total_num_tokens <= self.max_num_tokens failing inside the engine's request-preparation path [TRT-LLM] [E] Encountered an error in forward function, followed by an error in the event loop reporting that sampling failed The reported total exceeding the configured maximum by a handful of tokens rather than by a large margin The overshoot varying between runs, sometimes a few tokens and occasionally by thousands Disabling partial reuse making the failure arrive sooner rather than preventing it An assertion comparing a running token total against the configured maximum, firing under load The scheduler making no forward progress while requests remain queued Throughput collapsing to zero without any request completing or failing The condition appearing only above a threshold request rate and clearing on restart tensorrt-llm scheduler deadlock in-flight-batching token-budget concurrency serving Throughput reaches zero while the process stays up and keeps accepting connections It only appears above a certain request rate, so it never reproduces in a quiet environment An assertion about token accounting fires, which reads as an internal bug rather than saturation Restarting clears it until the load returns Admission is a resource-allocation decision made repeatedly against a shared budget. If a request's demand can grow after it has been admitted, the scheduler can reach a state where the total exceeds what it promised itself, with every admitted request needing more budget to finish and none able to release any. That is a deadlock in the classical sense rather than an overload: no participant can proceed and none will yield. It is why the server neither completes work nor sheds it, and why nothing times out on its own. It is load-dependent because the state requires a particular interleaving of admissions and completions. At low concurrency the budget is never contended tightly enough to reach it, which is why it survives testing and appears in production.

encyclopedia.action: Reduce the maximum batched token budget so the scheduler operates with headroom rather than at its ceiling, which removes the tight contention the state requires.
steps: Reduce the maximum batched token budget so the scheduler operates with headroom rather than at its ceiling, which removes the tight contention the state requires.
Lower the concurrent request limit, which bounds how many claims can be outstanding against the budget at once.
Disable features that let an admitted request's token demand grow, such as speculative decoding, while establishing whether they are involved.
Cap the served context length to the workload's real maximum so no single request can claim a large fraction of the budget.
Restart to restore service once the accounting has wedged, since nothing in the scheduler will unwind the state on its own, and treat that as mitigation rather than a fix.

encyclopedia.title: Mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine collectives time out on large NVLink domains
encyclopedia.text: Mixture-of-experts dispatch and combine collectives time out on large NVLink domains Communication torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: unspecified launch failure raised from torch.cuda.synchronize() The synchronize call being the frame that reports the fault, several operations after the exchange that actually stalled No collective named anywhere in the traceback, because the failing call is an ordinary device synchronisation A receive operation timing out during the dispatch or combine phase of expert routing The stall occurring inside an all-to-all exchange rather than an all-reduce Onset only at large NVLink domain sizes such as a full rack-scale system Progress halting mid-step with every rank waiting and none raising a fault mixture-of-experts expert-parallel all-to-all dispatch-combine nvl72 collective-timeout moe-routing The stall is inside a collective, so no rank has an error of its own to report It depends on the data, because routing decides the exchange volume, and so it appears irregularly It emerges at large domain sizes and cannot be reproduced on a smaller topology Both the routing and the transport look correct in isolation It frequently does not present as a timeout at all, and that is the hardest part of recognising it. When a collective is abandoned the communicator is torn down while its kernels are still resident on the device. The next call that inspects device state, commonly torch.cuda.synchronize at the end of a benchmark iteration, is the one that collects the wreckage, and it reports an unspecified launch failure. The frame in the traceback is therefore innocent, and the exchange that stalled has already been cleaned up by the time anything is printed. Expert routing makes communication data-dependent. Which ranks exchange how much is decided per step by the router, so the traffic pattern changes from step to step and is not the uniform, symmetric shape that collective implementations are usually tuned and tested against. All-to-all is the most demanding of those patterns because every rank talks to every other simultaneously. Scaling the domain multiplies the number of concurrent peer exchanges rather than adding to it, so resource limits and ordering assumptions that hold within a node can fail across a rack. The receive side is where it surfaces because that is the side that waits. A dispatch that was not sent, or was sent to a peer that had already moved on, leaves a receiver blocked with nothing to report except that its data did not arrive.

encyclopedia.action: Establish whether the stall is in dispatch or in combine, since they are separate exchanges with different volumes and narrowing to one halves the search.
steps: Establish whether the stall is in dispatch or in combine, since they are separate exchanges with different volumes and narrowing to one halves the search.
Reproduce at a smaller domain size to determine whether the fault scales with the number of peers, which distinguishes a topology-scale problem from a model or routing bug.
Fall back to a general-purpose collective implementation rather than the low-latency dispatch and combine path, which establishes whether the specialised kernel is involved.
Capture per-rank progress at the point of the stall so the exchange can be reconstructed; without it there is no record of which rank owed data to which.
Constrain routing so the per-step exchange is more uniform, for example by capping how many tokens any one expert may receive, which removes the extreme imbalances that stress the exchange hardest.

encyclopedia.title: Weights-only load failed with an UnpicklingError when you resume an older checkpoint
encyclopedia.text: Weights-only load failed with an UnpicklingError when you resume an older checkpoint Checkpointing _pickle.UnpicklingError: Weights only load failed, raised from inside the checkpoint loader WeightsUnpickler error: Unsupported global, naming a class such as an optimizer that was not an allowed global by default A suggestion to call add_safe_globals or use the safe_globals context manager with the named class Every rank raising the same error at the same point, because they are all reading the same common state weights-only unpickling torch-load add-safe-globals checkpoint optimizer-state distributed-checkpoint The file is intact and readable, so every corruption check comes back clean The same file loaded successfully under the previous framework release The message offers a way to disable the restriction, which is the fastest fix and the wrong default It surfaces at resume, typically hours into a queue slot, on every rank at once Reconstructing a pickle can execute arbitrary code, because the format stores instructions for rebuilding objects rather than only their data. Restricting the loader to tensors and primitives by default closes that hole, and it is the right default for a file arriving from anywhere but your own cluster. A training checkpoint is not only tensors. It holds the optimizer, its parameter groups, the scheduler, the sampler position and the run's arguments, all of which are Python objects that the restricted loader will not rebuild. The first one encountered stops the load, so the reported class is whichever came first and not necessarily the only one. Nothing is wrong with the checkpoint. It was written under a permissive default and is being read under a strict one, so the change of behaviour lives entirely in the reader. This is why file-level integrity checks all pass and why the same bytes still load in the older release.

encyclopedia.action: Allowlist the specific classes the checkpoint legitimately contains, using the serialization allowlist the error message names. This keeps the protection for everything else and is the fix that is safe to leave in place.
steps: Allowlist the specific classes the checkpoint legitimately contains, using the serialization allowlist the error message names. This keeps the protection for everything else and is the fix that is safe to leave in place.
Prefer the scoped context manager over a global registration when the allowlist is only needed around one load, so the relaxation does not outlive the call that needed it.
Read the whole error rather than the first line. It names the exact class it refused, and adding that one class is often the entire fix.
Where the checkpoint is your own and its provenance is not in question, disabling the restriction for that single load is defensible, but do it at the call site rather than as a process-wide setting.
Expect to repeat the allowlisting more than once: the load stops at the first unsupported class, so a second and third may appear behind it.

encyclopedia.title: Python 3.13 cannot pickle code objects, so a distributed job reports the wrong failure
encyclopedia.text: Python 3.13 cannot pickle code objects, so a distributed job reports the wrong failure Environment TypeError: cannot pickle code objects raised while an exception was being propagated between ranks The failure appearing inside object gathering or an object-to-tensor conversion rather than in training code A test asserting on an error message finding the pickling message instead of the one it expected Identical code succeeding on the previous interpreter minor version python-3.13 pickle compatibility version-mismatch interpreter-upgrade gather-object traceback The reported error is about pickling and has nothing to do with what actually went wrong The real exception is destroyed by the reporting path, so there is nothing to search for It only appears on the newer interpreter, so it reads as a framework bug rather than an environment change It surfaces on the error path, which by definition is the least exercised code in the system An extracted traceback is not a lightweight record. Its frames reference code objects, and code objects are compiled bytecode with no stable serialised representation, so pickling them was always questionable. The newer interpreter stops permitting it, which is a correctness decision rather than a regression. The failure lands on the reporting path specifically because that is the only place a traceback is deliberately carried around. Normal operation never pickles one, so an upgrade can pass every test and every training step and still break the moment something else fails. The consequence is a lost diagnosis rather than a lost job. Whatever genuinely failed raised first; the attempt to describe it to the other ranks raised second; and only the second one reaches the log.

steps: Convert the traceback to text at the point of capture and send the string. Formatting produces exactly what a human needs, and a string pickles everywhere.
Send the exception's type name and message as plain data alongside that text, so the receiving side can still branch on the kind of failure without reconstructing an object.
Look for the original error in the per-rank logs, which are written before the propagation attempt and therefore still contain it.
Pin the interpreter minor version for the cluster while the framework catches up, if the propagation path is not yours to change.
Where a framework is at fault, check whether it already formats tracebacks elsewhere; this is usually one call site that was missed rather than a design decision.

encyclopedia.title: Ray client connection aborts on ARM64 after a grpcio upgrade while x86 is unaffected
encyclopedia.text: Ray client connection aborts on ARM64 after a grpcio upgrade while x86 is unaffected Distributed Training ConnectionAbortedError: Initialization failure from server, raised from the client connect path RuntimeError: Starting Ray client server failed, naming a separate server log file for the detail The same image and configuration connecting reliably on x86_64 and intermittently on aarch64 Failures clustering after a transport library version changed rather than after any application change ray grpcio arm64 aarch64 version-mismatch compatibility ray-client transitive-dependency It is intermittent, so a retry succeeds and the upgrade looks innocent It is architecture-specific, so any x86 test environment reproduces nothing The client's error reports that the server failed, and the server's reason is elsewhere The library that changed is a transitive dependency nobody chose to upgrade The transport library ships architecture-specific binary wheels containing a large compiled core. The Python surface is identical across architectures and the compiled half is not, so a release can carry a defect that exists only in the ARM64 build and is invisible to testing done on x86. Session establishment is the most demanding moment for that channel: it negotiates, starts a server process, and exchanges configuration under a timeout. Marginal behaviour that a steady-state channel would absorb becomes a visible failure here, which is why it aborts at connect and not during work. The intermittency follows from a timing-sensitive handshake rather than from anything about the workload. A retry that succeeds is not evidence the upgrade is fine; it is evidence the failure is a race.
